*Look outside, not inside: a digital culture encourages employees to look outward and engage with customers and partners to develop new solutions.
*Prize delegation over control: a digital culture diffuses decision making throughout the organization.
*Encourage boldness over caution: a digital culture encourages people to take risks, fail fast, and learn.
*More action, less planning: a digital culture promotes speed and continuous iteration.
*Value collaboration over individual effort: a digital culture thrives on transparency and interaction. by The Boston Consulting Group (BCG)

This week, world leaders are gathered in New York to discuss the growing epidemic of tuberculosis (TB) and the increasing burden non-communicable diseases (NCDs), the first time in history that there are two High-Level Meetings on health during a UN General Assembly. These meetings are a pivotal opportunity to step up the pace to match the ambition of the 2030 Agenda
Progress and investments on both TB and NCDs to date remains insufficient.  TB infects more than 10 million new people every year and claims 4500 lives every day. NCDs account for 70 percent of the world’s deaths, killing 15 million people between the ages of 30 and 69 every year. At the same time, half the world lacks access to essential health services. 
UNDP is working with partners to drive multi-sectoral action and partnerships across government, the UN system, private sector, civil society and academia. For example, UNDP partners with the Global Fund to support and strengthen multi-sectoral responses to TB in 22 countries by providing integrated policy, programme and capacity development support. To date, this has resulted in 888,398 TB cases being successfully treated.  Increasing access to TB diagnosis and treatment, and ensuring no-one is ‘left behind’, is a priority. To raise awareness of these issues in the lead up to the high level meeting, we are communicating on our work in Tuvalu where UNDP, the Global Fund and the Red Cross are working closely with the Government to address the barriers to healthcare remote communities face , by bringing TB diagnosis and treatment directly into peoples communities and homes. #UNDP

The joint EU/UN $500 million-euro initiative will work to accelerate efforts to end violence against women and girls (EVAWG) around the world. The Spotlight Latin America programme, which will fund targeted interventions in five (5) Spotlight countries (Argentina, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico) to improve the rights of women and girls, helping them to live lives free from violence with a view to eradicating #femicide in Latin America. The Latin America programme will also include a regional component aimed at sharing the successful practices and lessons learnt, while replicating relevant programmes throughout the region.

In Latin America, UNDP has partnered with UN Women, UNFPA, UNICEF and other partner agencies, in a work that will focus on the elimination of the violence against women and girls, and in particular the fight against femicide, through strengthening and implementation of laws and public policies, work with state institutions to improve their response; prevention through evidence-based programs and campaigns, the establishment of essential services for victims and survivors; the collection and use of data on the prevalence and incidence of cases of violence against women and girls and quality, disaggregated and comparable femicides; and the work and strengthening of civil society organizations in their work in the elimination of violence against women and girls and femicide.

Specifically, UNDP will use its expertise and comparative advantage to support the adaptation and strengthening of normative frameworks and public policies for the elimination of VAWG and femicide, the strengthening of institutions in the generation and analysis of data that relate citizen security with violence against women and girls, including the adoption of an indicator of femicide. In addition, UNDP will make available to the countries of the region good practices and evidence to inform the design of public policies, for example, in situations of generalized violence; and strengthening the capacities of security and justice systems to provide services to victims.

Violence against women and girls is one of the most widespread and devastating human rights violations globally. I am pleased to share with you Issue 14 of the SIDS Bulletin, highlighting the leadership of SIDS in designing solutions for COVID-19 response and recovery, as well as commitments to climate action. 

https://lnkd.in/eGgWrPm

Despite the immense challenges that COVID-19 poses to SIDS, we continue to see strong action on accelerating sustainable development priorities aligned in the SAMOA Pathway. The AOSIS Placencia Ambition Forum reaffirmed that climate security lies at the heart of sustainability in SIDS, and that we must design our COVID-19 response to not only increase climate action and ambitions, but promote inclusive development. UNDP's Climate Promise seeks to strengthen this action, and is actively supporting 27 SIDS in developing their enhanced NDCs and in transforming their energy, transport and tourism sectors to reflect SIDS' climate stewardship and accelerate resilience building.

In this issue, we highlight various digital transformation and innovative financing mechanism that are vital our COVID-19 response and recovery efforts in SIDS, as well as success stories of SIDS operationalizing the three pillars of UNDP's Enhanced SIDS Offer.

Best regards and stay safe,
 Riad

What is the future of development?

The future is not what it used to be. A crisis can change the world from one day to the next, with tragic consequences.

But the actions countries take as they prepare, respond and recover in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic will lay the foundations for a fair and just transition to the future – a new social contract.

That is why, as the UN’s leading agency on development, UNDP is not working to help people “get back to normal”. Normal was not good enough.

With the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) as our compass, we want people to get back to something better – a future everyone believes in, where no one is left behind.

Four years in, mangroves are sprouting, populations of wildlife, shrimp, and fish are increasing, and flooding is more controlled

As we continue to have more conversations surrounding #digital finance in SIDS, I would like to highlight an important piece from our 23rd Bulletin.

Many had predicted that the rate of remittances in SIDS would fall during the pandemic. They account for an average of 10% of GDP in Pacific #SIDS; so, it would’ve been a devastating loss. However, the pandemic appears to have led to an uptick in digitally enabled remittances.

• Money sent to Fiji via the M-PAiSA Mobile Money app, developed by Vodafone with the support of the Pacific Financial Inclusion Programme (PFIP), quadrupled between February and August.
• ANZ Bank has announced that customers will be able to send payments from Australia and New Zealand to many Pacific Islands cost-free until February 2021.

This progress is encouraging. But we need to continue to address costs barriers to digital remittances — making the PFIP’s work (a partnership between UNDP  and @UNCDF) to support financial inclusion more crucial than ever.

Read an interview with Bram Peters, the Program Manager of PFIP here: https://ab.co/3nBjcEu

Agricultural expansion to achieve food security in Small #Island Developing States has the potential to negatively impact their environments, damaging biodiversity and vulnerable ecosystems. Right now, the world’s agriculture systems make up 10% of #carbon emissions.  

So, as we strive for reliable, nutritious food sources in #SIDS, we should also be exploring greener agriculture models. In our 23rd UNDP SIDS Bulletin, we featured the exciting potential of #smartfarming and #artificialntelligence technology to feed the hungry and preserve our environment through: 
1- #Data collection for improved farming efficiency 
2- Reinvented farming techniques (such as computer algorithms for detecting harvest times) 
3-Indoor farming 
4-Plant-based production 

#Digital transformation through #AI is a promising path forward to improve both agricultural productivity and sustainability in SIDS.

Precision agriculture is a data-driven approach to farming that addresses the needs of individual farms.

Working Session Recap

Last week, in collaboration with AUDA NEPAD, we hosted a working session in Stellenbosch for our project launched earlier this year titled “Africa’s Development Agenda for its Green Minerals”.

This project has brought together scholars to craft policy papers and briefs to analyze African governments' plans for mineral-driven industrialization and manufacturing. This included in-depth country case studies, exploring ambitious mineral strategies and their essential requirements, such as the DRC-Zambia battery industry MoU, South Africa's PGM endeavors, and Zimbabwe's lithium-powered ambitions.

The working session was a platform to discuss the findings and progress of the papers and chart the course for the next phase of the project.
A special acknowledgment to Mkhululi N Ncube from African Minerals Development  Centre  (AMDC) and Melaku Desta of Africa Trade Policy Centre at UNECA for their invaluable contributions as discussion facilitators.

Our gratitude goes out to Pamla Gopaul, Axel Rusenga, and Dr. Mustafa Sakr of AUDA NEPAD for pleasantly hosting us. We especially thank Saliem Fakir of The African Climate Foundation and Fred Kabanda of African Development Bank Group for their valuable presence.

A big thank you to our project leads, Dr. Olumide Abimbola, Patience, Amir Lebdioui, and all the contributors who have dedicated their expertise to this project.

We will continue to use this space to share project updates in due course!

🌍 Inspired by the Youth4Climate: #SparkingSolutions Event
 
Last week, I had the privilege of being part of the selection panel for the Energy thematic at the Youth4Climate: Sparking Solutions event in Rome. Witnessing the passion, dedication, and innovative spirit of the youth presenting their energy projects was truly remarkable.
 
Gathering from 63 countries, these young minds came together with a 100 youth-driven solutions, all with a shared goal of creating a meaningful impact on our planet. The level of creativity and thoughtfulness in their projects was truly impressive.
 
At the event, I had the honor of witnessing some incredible project pitches from the youth. These innovative solutions included ideas such as harnessing affordable and renewable heating sources like Biomass, a high-performing stove that can save up to 5 tons of CO2 emissions, and initiatives to promote the use of solar power in off-grid schools and community centres. These ideas are not only impressive but also represent tangible steps towards reducing our carbon footprint and promoting #cleanenergy solutions. It's a testament to their dedication and ingenuity.
 
Taking part in the #Youth4Climate event reaffirmed my conviction: the future of our planet is in the hands of the next generation, and they are ready to take on the challenge. But we need to empower them, provide the support they need, and enable them to implement  their ideas so that #sustainableenergy use becomes the norm, not the exception.
 
The #Youth4Climate initiative, co-led by the UNDP Rome Centre  and Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica  funding, mentorship programs, and capacity-building opportunities, these young climate leaders will have the tools to turn their innovative ideas into reality.

#EnergyForDevelopment

My new  book, “Revisiting the Ocean: Living the Blue Economy” builds on the foundation laid in my previous work, “Rethinking the Oceans”. In this sequel, I reinforce the idea that the Ocean is a valuable ecosystem that can drive sustainable economic growth while ensuring its health and protection.
It is no secret that the greater part
our planet is the sea. Yet we continue to treat it as less important than land. The Ocean is our greatest hope for the future. It is time we see it for what it is. My book urges us to do just that. I realise the challenges we face as well as to the multitude of wonderful initiatives. Whether we focus on new sources of renewable energy, or the work of volunteers restoring our beaches and protecting wildlife; whether it is the immense contribution that can be made by the inventive use of seaweed, or business startups for which nothing is impossible - all mark a turning of the tide. We should take heed. If we are willing to put our trust in the Ocean, we can yet win the day. 
My new book -“Revisiting the Ocean - Living the Blue Economy” is a book of hope !

Last month, a BIG news came out of the palm oil industry, with significant (positive) implications for the wider agri-commodities sector!

The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) announced the appointment of a tripartite consortium comprising of leading agritech firms Agridence , CIED , and NGIS “to develop a unified, bespoke Certification, Trade, and Traceability System (CTTS)”.

The keyword here – at least for me – is ‘traceability’, which has been a longstanding challenge for the industry. This is because of complex supply chains and difficulties in tracking palm oil from small-scale producers, who make up a large part of the commodity production.

RSPO’s revamped digital system would essentially aim to streamline and integrate RSPO’s sustainable palm oil certification, audit, and risk assessment processes into a secure trading platform, enabling end-to-end traceability of palm oil.

This comes as a major relief to palm oil corporates, who are under pressure from the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which will come into effect from December 2024. EUDR mandates that importers of deforestation-risk commodities (e.g., palm oil, cocoa, timber, natural rubber) and their derived products into the EU market must be able to prove that the products do not originate from recently deforested or degraded land.

The new system to be developed by the consortium, led by Singapore-based Agridence, could be instrumental for demonstrating the sustainable origin of RSPO-certified palm oil, especially from major producers Indonesia and Malaysia. The system will leverage Agridence’s experience and expertise from building a similar platform for the natural rubber industry.

At Singapore Agri-Food Innovation Lab (SAIL) , we are engaged in exploring innovations, learnings, and best practices from different industries and supporting their adaptation and adoption by our Corporate Partners and stakeholders to drive sustainability in the wider agri-food sector.

History was made on the first day of the UN Climate Conference, #COP28 . UNDP Maldives welcomes the historic agreement to operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund and funding arrangements and acknowledges the unwavering efforts made by Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) and the Maldivian Government with its members of the transitional committee who worked tirelessly to get us to this point.

In conjunction with this momentous development, we are delighted to present a new paper titled 'Loss and Damage and Climate Litigation: How Can the Maldives and other Small Island Developing States (SIDS) Position Itself for Greater Climate Action.' Authored by UNDP Maldives in collaboration with Frankfurt School of Finance & Management , the paper advocates for a unified climate governance strategy, empowering vulnerable SIDS like the Maldives with reforms and strategic options to embrace this innovative instrument of climate justice now in action.

The paper explores the critical nexus between climate-related loss and damage and the recent surge in climate litigation. It argues that SIDS should lead robust and equitable climate action, navigating the complex relationship between climate change, human rights, and legal responsibilities. The paper advocates for enhanced funding for SIDS, rooted in the principles of loss and damage, utilizing both traditional and novel financing mechanisms.

The recommendations within the paper urge #SIDS to spearhead climate resilience initiatives, employing innovative financial and insurance strategies. It underscores the need for exhaustive data collection and risk assessments to strengthen early warning systems and devise disaster risk strategies. To effectively manage and foresee climate litigation risks, it calls for educational initiatives on climate liability, incentivization of private sector adaptation, and harmonization of national legal frameworks with environmental pledges.

The overarching aim is to develop a cohesive approach that integrates financial risk management, climate adaptation, and active engagement in the development of international climate finance mechanisms. While primarily intended for the Maldives, the insights also hold relevance for other nations.

Reflecting on #COP28 in Dubai, it's evident that the conference signifies a crucial starting point, but substantial efforts are still imperative to avert a 1.5°C temperature rise. The urgency transcends mere negotiations; it underscores the need to secure financing promptly for a swift transition to a decarbonized world.

At the core of achieving decarbonization objectives lies the imperative to minimize risks and their associated costs, emphasizing the pressing nature of the situation. The clarion call is unequivocal—intensify endeavors in renewables, triple efficiency, and substantially augment climate finance.

Acknowledging the magnitude of the challenge, reliance on public finance alone proves inadequate. This is an all-encompassing moment that requires collaboration with both multilateral and national development banks to strengthen their role in channeling and delivering climate finance along with domestic and international public and private finance. Equally pivotal is the active engagement of the private sector in steering this transformative journey. 

On the COP sidelines, discussions with officials from Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Maldives, Nepal, Ethiopia, Vietnam, Zimbabwe, Senegal, Azerbaijan and Togo, along with UNDP representation at key events, underscored a shared vision for change. From elevating ambitions in NBSAPs to championing nature-based solutions and just energy transformation, the common thread is clear—change is possible and already underway.

This year has been a testament to the dedication, resilience, and impact of our initiative as we achieved a significant milestone. Our delegation, comprising ten fellows from various Arab countries, effectively implemented our programs, a testament to our commitment to climate action and sustainable development. The journey to COP28 UAE  was enriched by our pre-conference efforts, notably our participation in the #menaclimateweek held in Riyadh. The successful implementation of our programs and the meaningful engagement of our 10 fellows at COP28 underscore our commitment to representing diverse voices, especially those from regions facing conflict, occupation, or marginalization.

Central to our preparatory phase were comprehensive capacity-building sessions. These sessions, led by experts like Mr. Kamal Djemouai  on negotiation principles and Riad Meddeb  alongside his team at the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub, focused on just transitions and green jobs. But also some sessions on leadership skills sessions by other partners. This groundwork was crucial in equipping our fellows with the necessary skills and knowledge to navigate the complexities of climate negotiations and advocacy.

At COP28, our primary focus was on fostering meaningful engagement for our current fellows as well as alumnus. We created platforms enabling them to voice the concerns and aspirations of their communities.This approach ensured that diverse perspectives were represented and heard, an essential aspect of inclusive and effective climate action.

As we conclude this year’s mission, our eyes are set on the future. We are already laying the groundwork for next year’s initiatives. We are deeply committed to sustaining and expanding our programs, and in this spirit, we are open to exploring partnerships and collaborations. 

We believe that through collective effort and shared knowledge, we can create a more sustainable and equitable future. Therefore, we warmly invite you to join us in this endeavor. Your support, be it through expertise, resources, fund, capacity building, or advocacy, would be invaluable in our journey towards a just greener, more resilient world. 

Absolutely, a heartfelt thank you is due to everyone who played a part in this year’s success. Our partners’ invaluable contributions and our fellows who deserve immense appreciation for their dedication and enthusiasm. And of course, a special acknowledgment to our own team Neeshad Shafi  Amal Ridene  and Omnia El Omrani, MD  Small in size but monumental in impact, each member’s dedication, creativity, and perseverance have been the cornerstone of our achievements.

This year of success is not just an end but a beacon for future endeavors, inspiring us to continue our journey with more vigor and determination.

The cat is out of the bag: My book "Survival of the Greenest" is officially coming out on May 20th 2024.

The main message of the book is simple: Regardless of a nation's responsibility for climate change, the ability to develop is tied to the climate agenda. #AI for #ClimateAction- A balancing act between opportunities & perils of artificial intelligence in #climatechange. 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn
 
I am excited to share my new podcast on “AI solutions for Cimate Actions & Insights from #COP28 with @Carina Schuster 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn  
@Sci-Tech Suisse Podcast
 
AI can do great things to fight climate change:
 
✅ The use of data-driven AI solutions can produce starting results in the fight against climate change
 
✅ Data and AI platforms can be powerful instruments to predict weather, track #GHG emission or develop targeted strategies against #airpollution or support the protection of #biodiversity and endangered #species

✅ AI tolls can accurately predict the #deforestation of #rainforest and loss of biodiversity though the analysis of aerial photographs and #satellite data

✅ AI can be used to enhance the #sustainability of #agriculture, lower #airpollution or reduce negative environmental impact of infrastructure projects
  
AI can become a huge problem for climate change:
 
✅The use of AI technologies is expected to grow exponentially with the expected growth of the current global AI #market size of around $200 billion U.S. dollars to reach over 1.8 trillion U.S. dollars by 2030.

✅ #Machinelearning and the training of AI #algorithms require huge amount of computing power and #electricity

✅ The #computing #power required for AI applications, such as recognizing & processing images and vast among of data increased 300,000-fold from 2012 to 2018.

✅AI and #Deeplearning require huge amount of high-quality data and increasingly huge computing power and data #infrastructure

✅The training one AI model using a single high-end graphics card (#gpu ) generates the carbon equivalent of a flight across the United States or 626,000 pounds of carbon dioxide (MIT Technology Review

Huge Public Investments in AI for Good is needed to leverage the power of AI for climate action

✅ Increasingly AI models require and deep learning require huge computing power driven by specialized computer chips- called GPUs

✅ The costs of the needed AI infrastructure in the form of hyperscale #datacenters and data infrastructure are becoming huge

✅ Whereby #bigtech companies, such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft are investing billions into AI the public sector, research institutions and universities don’t have the necessary resources to make the necessary huge investments

✅ AI can only be unleased for climate action through public sector investments, since the big tech companies are purely focused on commercial applications of AI

✅ A large boost in public concessional #climatefinance is needed since only a very small part of private sector investments go into the development of AI models for the public good & AI to for climate action.

I am absolutely honored to be selected as an IRENA Youth Delegate for 2024. 
 
I am thrilled to be among the 100 IRENA Youth Delegates from 60 different countries, The New Generation of Decision Makers at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Youth Forum at the 14th IRENA Assembly in Abu Dhabi, UAE. 
The program kicked off with a welcoming session led by the Director-General of IRENA and esteemed guests, followed by panel discussions covering various topics focused on fostering engagement in key technological advancements, building capacity for #youth at the core of the energy transition, providing #opportunities for youth to play a key role in #IRENA's mission of accelerating #renewableenergy deployment, achieving climate objectives, and advancing the #sustainable development agenda.

Over the first days of the forum, we had an enlightening introduction on topics in #finance, #science, #social, and #policy aspects in renewable energy. We had presentation about introduction to renewable energy by Cesar Barraza-Botet, PhD  covering renewable energy sources from solar to wind, hydrogen, and new innovations in the sector. Other sessions included skills development for the energy transition by Samah Elsayed, discussions on ESGs and Social Corporate Responsibility for a just energy transition by AbdelRahman Fahmy  and Asma Rouabhia, and skills youth need in developing renewable energy projects and proposals by AbdelRahman Fahmy and David Arinze 

On the second day of the forum, I attended the session with IEEE , Advancing Technology for Humanity works on #AI for #DigitalInnovations in Energy transitions with speakers Sajith Wijesuriya, Krishna Ajith  and  Cybele Ghanem.    

The Forum continued with a panel discussion including #AcceleratingYouthLedInnovationandEntrepreneurshipinCleanTechPanel, with panelists, Grace Nanteza, Asma Rouabhia, Nourhan Algharabli, Benjamin Keller  and Shreshth Mishra, who shared the challenges and barriers faced by youth-led innovations. 

There inspiring thoughts, experiences, and advice addressed the true skills that all young changemakers  need to have, emphasizing the importance of being ready to #failfast, Having the #courage to continue until we achieve success as well as creating as many #connections as possible. 
I had the opportunity to share about renewable energy projects to  powering agriculture and the potential of #Agrivoltaics,  integrating the  #food production and #energy generation, the Food-Energy-Water nexus.  

The IRENA Youth Forum were filled with #encouragement with inspirational closing by from Riccardo Toxiri and Riad Meddeb.  I look forward to the #IRENAAssembly and the #FutureEnergyForum in the coming days which IRENA Youth delegates have the opportunity to meet with global leaders, government representatives, and IRENA experts.

#IRENA #RenewableEnergy #YouthLeadership #SDGs  #Sustainability #ClimeteAction  #YouthEmpowerment  #EnergyTransition #EnergyEfficiency

Meeting His Excellency Dr. Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, CEO ADNOC Group, President COP28 UAE, Chairman Masdar (Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company), and Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology for UAE, was no less than a dream come true! Last week, I had the incredible honour of serving as the official Youth Representative at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) (A United Nations Organisation) Youth Forum: The New Generation of Decision Makers, the IRENA 14th Assembly, and the World Future Energy Summit in Abu Dhabi. 

Throughout these events, I engaged with diplomats, ministers, and policymakers from across the globe, discussing the challenges and opportunities in the transition to sustainable energy. It was enlightening to see the world come together with a shared goal of fostering a cleaner, more sustainable future. Moderating a live session and questioning Riad Meddeb, Director of Sustainability Hub, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), about bridging the gap between youth, financing, and renewable energy was one of the major highlights.

I was particularly inspired by the diversity and passion of the other youth delegates—over 150 of us chosen from a pool of 57,000 applicants. Together, we exchanged ideas, learned from one another, and advocated for the integration of youth perspectives in shaping global energy policies.

The insights gained and the connections made have profoundly impacted my understanding of global energy dynamics. I am grateful for the opportunity to represent youth interests at such a high level and am more committed than ever to contributing to our sustainable future.

📣 Exciting News For SIDS & Nature 🏝️

At SIDS4, during the Blue & Green Islands Reception co-hosted by UNDP and Global Environment Facility , the Government of Belize🇧🇿 (co-lead of the SIDS Coalition for Nature ) just announced the planned collaboration between the SIDS Coalition for Nature & the GEF 8-funded Blue and Green Island Integrated Programme (GBI IP). This key collaboration has been facilitated by the SIDS Unit of United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs .

This promising partnership responds to the Coalition’s Call For Action made at Biodiversity COP15 in Montreal with UN DSG support. Three areas of cooperation will shape the strategic partnership between the Coalition and the GEF Program: 1/ Partnership Development coordination, including SIDS-SIDS cooperation; 2/ Strategic advocacy, and 3/ National-Regional implementation support to bridge knowledge and financing gaps for integrated nature action in SIDS. 

Synergies between GEF-8 GBI IP ‘child’ projects and various Coalition’s initiatives will also be sought. This will be the case for the a.o. Delighted to have delivered a keynote at the Round Table Discussion, organized by ISA with the EU and SolarPower Europe, on transforming Africa through sustainable energy & partnerships, where I emphasized the urgent need to evolve our financing approach to address disparities in clean energy finance in Africa.

Currently, investments are unevenly distributed, with ten nations accounting for 90% of private energy infrastructure investment. This leaves annual financing needs for energy access initiatives far short of the required $25B USD to achieve the 2030 objectives. In 2024, an estimated $110B USD will be invested in energy across Africa, with $70B allocated to fossil fuels and only 35% to clean energy technologies.

In my address, I highlighted the three key levers for systemic transformation:

1. To shift the focus of finance at the national level, which still prioritizes risks to lenders over the greater risk that climate change poses to people & the planet.
2. Changing the macro-level financial system to facilitate access to capital in critical geographies and sectors.
3. Optimizing energy systems with AI-driven solutions to boost renewable energy investment where its needed most.

Around 60 million people in Africa 🌍access electricity via off-grid solutions, with 15 countries using distributed renewables in their electrification plans. Scaling renewable, decentralized, and affordable energy systems can drive inclusive development.

Establishing robust financial models and fostering public-private partnerships are key to unlocking the $200 billion annual investment needed by 2030 for Africa's energy, climate, and development goals.

Delighted to have participated in the ‘Let’s Talk Data’ event with experts from @worldbank, @universityofmichigan, and @UNDP. 

I emphasized on the human angle of sustainable energy for development, and the need to go beyond collecting data, making these findings actionable for amplifying our impact on the ground:

* Energy poverty affects health, social inclusion, and economic opportunities. We must prioritize data and indicators that include social, environmental and development dimensions
* Open energy modeling tools need to better incorporate social and development factors beyond market dynamics. We must invest in data infrastructure to address urban-rural disparities, informal energy markets, economic transitions, and disaggregated demographic data.
* Effective energy policies and interventions require precise, actionable insights derived from high-resolution geospatial data and advanced analytics, enabling equitable interventions to ensure renewable energy benefits reach all communities, especially underserved areas

At @UNDP, our focus remains on leveraging technology and data combined with an integrated development approach to achieve #SDG7 🌍

In recent years, amid alarming geopolitical turmoil and a global pandemic, the inherent vulnerabilities of traditional energy sources have been starkly exposed to the developed world. 

For many developing nations, however, price volatility, supply shortages, and geopolitical dependencies are not temporary disruptions but enduring realities. 

The transition to a renewables-based energy system addresses many of those issues, moving energy dependencies from the global to the regional level and making most countries less susceptible to geopolitical disruptions. 

However, while energy security options will become more diverse, the energy system will also grow more complex, given the wide range of technologies and participants involved. 

As governments make substantial investments in infrastructure that is increasingly electrified, digitalised, and decentralised, it is essential that decision makers do not simply transpose outdated paradigms from the fossil fuel era onto these emerging systems.

IRENA's report, "Geopolitics of the Energy Transition: Energy Security", explores specific issues that should be systematically considered to guide national decision-making in navigating the existing and emergent challenges of a highly complex and integrated new energy system. 👇

Today, 600 million people in Africa still live without electricity. 

Studies have shown it is the best predictor of whether someone can escape poverty. The Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative has highlighted the correlation between lack of electricity access and poor health, unemployment, malnourishment, and more. 

To address this, I am honored to announce that The Rockefeller Foundation is supporting Mission 300 (M300), an initiative of the World Bank Group and African Development Bank (AfDB) to provide electricity access to 300 million Africans by 2030. 

Alongside the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet (GEAPP), the @Rockefeller Foundation is committing an initial $10 million for the Mission 300 TA Accelerator, which will boost the projects needed to double the current pace of electrification on the continent.

Former U.S. Government Head of the Power Africa initiative, @Andrew Herscowitz, is also on board to help steer the M300 effort. 

We believe that by identifying innovative solutions, working with additional partners, and measuring our progress in initiatives such as M300, we can help African leaders usher in a period of green, inclusive growth. #PoweringAfrica

The Many Facets of Energy Transition: From India to the World

While the world has made progress in renewable energy deployment, with over 40 per cent of the world's electricity generated from zero-carbon sources (Source: BloombergNEF), taking clean energy to the last mile remains a problem. 

However, India, which ranks fourth globally in renewable energy installed capacity, stands out as a pioneer in the Global South with its energy transition story.  It has facilitated access to clean cooking fuels for over 96 million women in merely three years; the rural electrification programme has brought electricity to over 28 million households in a span of two years. The rooftop solar programme launched this year, ‘PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana’, aims to bring the benefits of solar energy to 10 million households across rural and urban areas. 

What lessons can the world take from India’s citizen-centric, sustainable, clean energy transition? How does access to clean energy intersect with other factors such as health, gender, and economic progress?

Our session with @SEforALL at UNEnergy’s #SDG7 Action Forum delved into these questions. Swipe to see what our speakers said!

After the first two days of the Global Off-Grid Solar Forum and Expo ( #GOGSFE24 ) in Nairobi, Kenya, some clear key messages are being shared with one voice across all stakeholders, including policymakers, industry leaders, business associations, development partners, and civil society organizations (CSOs):

1. Off-grid renewable energy solutions are the most cost-effective way to bridge the energy access gap while driving significant sustainable development benefits.
2. The business and financial models to address high financing costs already exist—there’s no need to reinvent the wheel.
3. Enforceable policy and regulatory frameworks are critical for unlocking private capital and scaling off-grid renewable energy solutions.
4. It is essential to integrate off-grid renewable energy solutions into broader energy sector planning.
5. Addressing the local currency financing challenges is fundamental to expanding off-grid renewable energy solutions.

A recurring theme through all these points is the need for deliberate partnerships among key stakeholders—no single partner can do it all. This is why I’m excited about how the African Minigrid Programme's building blocks will feed into the bold M300 initiative by the World Bank, the African Development Bank, and other partners.

We have the blueprint to address the energy access gap, and now is the time to implement it. Let’s roll up our sleeves and move forward boldly, together, to bring real change to the ground. Africa Minigrids Program

Today, I am raising the alarm.
 
Together with the Troika of COP28 UAE, COP29 Azerbaijan, COP30 Brazil Presidencies and the Global Renewables Alliance (GRA), IRENA published a report that tracks progress towards tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.

And as the custodian agency tasked with tracking and reporting on progress towards 2030, IRENA concludes that progress falls short. 

The landmark #UAEConsensus agreed at COP28 is critical for our global efforts to keep 1.5°C within reach but we are at risk of missing our collective goal.

Some key facts:

1- Despite an unprecedented growth in renewable power additions of 473 GW in 2023, it is far from enough. The world must add on average 1044 GW every year. 

2- Current Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) will only add 1.5 TW of renewable power capacity by 2030, but we need more than 7 TW.
 
3- Global investments in renewables reached a record of USD 570 billion in 2023 but it must triple to USD 1.5 trillion annually. 

Furthermore, current investment patterns are disproportionately concentrated in advanced economies and a few large emerging markets like China, India, and Brazil. The rest of the developing world remains underserved, receiving just 10% of global energy investments. This imbalance threatens not only the pace of energy transition but also the equitable distribution of its benefits.
 
It is still possible to achieve our goals, but it requires immediate global action to overcome the structural and systemic barriers that impede progress. Significant progress is needed across key enablers of the energy transition, namely: infrastructure and system operation, policy, supply chains and skills, finance and international collaboration. 

The next round of NDCs in 2025 must close the gaps. And an agreement on a robust New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) of climate finance at COP29 will be vital for enhancing financial support for climate action in the Global South.

Read ‘Delivering on the UAE Consensus: Tracking progress toward tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030’ that was released today at the PreCOP to inform national delegations and negotiators in the run up to COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. 👇

👉 Redirect investment: Global renewable investments of USD 570 billion must rise to USD 1.5 trillion annually to meet demand, with a focus on equitable finance for underserved nations.

In a major step toward healthcare resilience, UNDP  Zimbabwe and the The Global Fund  have equipped 1,044 health facilities across Zimbabwe with solar systems, with a combined generation capacity exceeding 11 MW. 🏥

This renewable energy solution ensures consistent power for rural clinics, enabling them to refrigerate vaccines, run essential medical equipment, and deliver uninterrupted patient care—even during power outages. By reducing grid dependency, this project addresses energy poverty and enhances healthcare access for underserved communities across Zimbabwe. 💡

Other key benefits of the solar project include:

1. Energy Efficiency: Solar systems provide up to 70% of electricity needs, reducing reliance on the grid.
2. Environmental Impact: Over 11,447 tons of CO2 emissions will be avoided annually.
3. Cost Savings: Cuts electricity and diesel costs, allowing more resources for healthcare services.

L'Algérie au sommet des Nations Unies sur la Biodiversité #COP16 🇩🇿🇺🇳

L'Algérie est souvent associée avec ses reserves petrolières... mais c'est aussi un grand reservoir de biodiversité! L'Algérie abrite une grande diversité d'habitats et d'écosystèmes dans les zones humides et dans le Sahara, notamment au sein des espaces protégés (dont un giga-espace de 633 887 km2 abritant le Massif du Hoggar!!!).

En tant qu'algériens, nous avons donc notre rôle à jouer dans les enjeux mondiaux de protection de la nature, etant donné les fortes menaces qui pèsent sur notre ecosysteme.

Merci donc aux hôtes Colombiens de la COP16 et à Escuela Superior de Administración Pública d'avoir mis l'accent sur notre pays afin d'évoquer notre rôle dans l'agenda de biodiversité et les relations entre la Colombie et l'Algerie, qui n'ont jamais été meilleures qu'aujourd'hui.

As COP16 Colombia  on biodiversity begins, we have an opportunity to show how renewable energy can support both climate action and biodiversity conservation.

Scaling up renewable energy is imperative for mitigating climate change, and with careful planning, it can enhance biodiversity protection. By deploying renewable solutions like wind, solar, and photovoltaics that incorporate biomimicry—mimicking natural processes such as the efficiency of photosynthesis—we can create energy nature-based solutions that harmonize with local habitats, solving electricity access challenges while safeguarding ecosystems. 🌱

Through strategic environmental assessments, renewable energy projects can do more than just power communities—they can reduce carbon emissions, protect habitats, and minimize disruption to fragile ecosystems. This dual approach enables us to tackle the climate and biodiversity crises together, aligning with our Kunming-Montreal Framework commitments. 🌳

60% of electricity in Latin America and the Caribbean is already generated from #renewables, double the global average. With abundant hydropower, solar PV, and wind potential, along with 60% of the world’s lithium reserves essential for battery technology, the region has the capacity to leverage this transition to redefine sustainable development while securing local benefits for its communities. 

Moreover, this shift also promises employment opportunities, with #energy sector jobs projected to increase by over 15% by 2030, particularly in clean energy technologies and in the critical mineral sector. This approach can extend beyond energy production to include key areas like transport electrification and sustainable mining, positioning LAC as a global blueprint for just energy transitions at scale. With COP16 and the Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) Energy Week now underway, LAC can maintain and accelerate their momentum toward a sustainable, resilient future powered by clean energy.

The #PactForTheFuture has been adopted, positioning energy access and security as essential for economic development, social stability, and achieving our Development Goals. It calls for urgent action to mobilize finance at scale to ensure affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy for all, alongside investments in resilient cross-border energy infrastructure.

Unlocking the scale of private investment in clean energy will require policy de-risking mechanisms to enhance the financial viability of renewable projects, incentivizing private capital, affordable tariffs, and expanded energy services. Given that 40% of low- and middle-income countries are facing severe debt issues, targeted financial flows and equitable redistribution are essential for accelerating renewable energy deployment in the Global South. #Digital , AI, and data hold immense potential to meet these goals by guiding financing towards impactful solutions through data-driven insights.

Monday, at COP29 Azerbaijan in Baku, UNDP and the Italian Ministry for Environment and Energy Security (Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica) hosted a panel of experts from African governments, the private sector, and DFIs to address Africa's untapped #RenewableEnergy potential and the essential need for financing in this sector.

Alessandro Guerri, Director General at Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica , and Riad Meddeb, Director of UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub, opened the event communicating the shared commitment of the MEES and UNDP to clean energy based development in Africa. 

Panellists:

✅ Edson Uamusse, member of the Board in Energy Fund (FUNAE)
✅ Esther Muringo Wang’ombe, Director Renewable Energy at the Ministry of Energy of Kenya
✅ Laura Muñoz Pérez, United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) Regional Manager for West Africa
✅ Avinash Persaud, Special Advisor on Climate Change to the President of the Inter-American Development Bank
✅ Oscar Njuguna, Group Director, Sustainability at Equity Bank Limited.

The speakers emphasised how partnerships are vital in developing, de-risking, and financing #CleanEnergy projects across Africa. Through #EnergyForGrowth in Africa, UNDP aims to leverage its on-the-ground expertise and coordinate infrastructure initiatives to transform Africa's clean energy sector, fostering growth and sustainability.

Thank you to our partners, speakers, and panellists who contributed to an inspiring discussion on how concessional finance and technical assistance can unlock capital, build strong investment environments, and advance Africa’s clean energy agenda.

✨🌍 Reflections from COP29 in Azerbaijan 
After four days at COP29, the atmosphere here is a mix of global urgency and local realities. UN Secretary-General António Guterres set a sombre tone in the opening session: “2024 is a masterclass of climate destruction.”

Our collective ambitions to #3xRenewables is critical to keep 1.5°C within reach. However, current NDCs cover only 12% of this target, and with the next round of NDCs due in 2025, this offers an opportunity to place advancing an energy transition as a priority for NDCs. ☀️

On the session “Pathways to Energy Integration in NDCs,” co-hosted by @‌IRENA and @Ocean Conservancy, I highlighted three key opportunities to make NDCs ambitious and actionable, focusing on scaling sustainable renewable energy:

1. Support countries in creating bankable energy projects integrated with their NDCs, ensuring these plans are actionable and backed by comprehensive sectoral investment analyses.
2. ⁠Promote financial innovation & implement tools like credit guarantees and blended finance, facilitating debt-smart energy transition financing in developing countries.
3. ⁠Leverage digital technologies to help identify optimal investment opportunities, ensure optimized off-grid solutions & enable data-driven policymaking.

UNDP  and United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  are supporting these efforts by scaling up capital for renewable energy and developing innovative guarantee schemes that provide safety nets for investors and lenders, reducing perceived risks to move renewable energy projects from pipeline to financial closure.

Clean cooking signifies more than just technological change; it is a powerful catalyst for a domino effect of outcomes – improved health, environmental protection, and economic empowerment. Yet, 2.1 billion people still depend on polluting and harmful fuels for this basic need. 

Recognizing this urgent challenge, G20 leaders at G20 Brasil 2024 this week reaffirmed their commitment to accelerate efforts to achieve universal clean cooking access by 2030. ☀️

With over 90% of people without clean cooking access also lacking the funding and policy environments for effective interventions, the ‘Roadmap for the Brazil G20 Presidency’s Clean Cooking Strategy’’—to which UNDP is honored to have contributed feedback—addresses these gaps by outlining actionable guidance to establish enabling policies and achieve universal clean cooking access by 2030 through four key pillars:

1. Enhancing policy and regulatory frameworks
2. Identifying and scaling innovative financing models
3. Strengthening markets and developing robust clean cooking supply chains
4. Assessing impact, sharing knowledge, and collecting data to support decision-making

Achieving universal clean cooking is within reach but demands strong political will. Success hinges on integrating clean cooking into climate pledges and national electrification strategies while mobilizing the $8 billion annually needed through data-driven policies, innovative financing, and collaboration between governments, NGOs, the private sector, and the communities we aim to empower. 💡

Let me reflect on Nadya Daulay's and my COP 29 mission from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Indonesia. There are at least two things that we brought to this event:

1. A larger blended finance platform at the regional or multilateral level requires a national-led platform to connect with. At the AIFC (Astana International Financial Centre) session at their nice pavilion, we thought cooperation between global southern countries was necessary. Still, domestic readiness should be prioritized to benefit more from a larger platform. This is the very reason why the G20 Bali Global Blended Finance Alliance aims to support a country-led platform in developing countries.
2. Developing countries should not perceive Carbon Border Adjustment as the core competitiveness problem. The real challenge is the global market is going green. Without taking necessary steps, such as decarbonizing the existing industry and developing the green industry, developing countries will never catch up with the trends and lose important global markets.

We actually got more than we brought. For instance, we successfully supported Ibu Mari Elka Pangestu and the G20 Bali Global Blended Finance Alliance to sign its cooperation with new knowledge partners and country members. We also met wonderful people with whom we could take pictures and learn from. We are grateful to meet my Columbia | SIPA Professor Jeffrey Sachs and David Sandalow; my UNDP's Sustainable Energy Hub Director and mentors Riad Meddeb, Simone Marino, and Stefano Pistolese; Jo Tyndall, Ma Jun; and our colleagues who have invited us to share our research Patricia Fuller, Alice Tipping, International Institute for Sustainable Development, AIFC (Astana International Financial Centre), and Asian Development Bank (ADB), and many other good friends and colleagues that we met, but we could not mention.

Thank you to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Indonesia, especially Dandy Rafitrandi, Mba Ira Setianti, Via Azlia Widiyadi, and Mas Yose Rizal Damuri. 

Also, Thanks for your support in any way you did. Even though the final result of the NCQG from COP 29th is not as satisfying as I expected, the effort of those people I met (who really fought for humanity against climate change at the COP, not those who came and did otherwise) should be appreciated. Climate progress, however small it is, should be something that we are grateful for. Keep fighting!

1️⃣ Financial Institutions: Innovative mechanisms such as blended finance, green bonds, and guarantees are essential to de-risk investments, mobilize capital, and scale solutions in high-risk regions.

2️⃣ Private Sector: The private sector plays a pivotal role in developing bankable renewable energy projects, mitigating risks, and fostering sustainable growth.

3️⃣ Media as a Catalyst: By amplifying success stories, media bridges gaps between stakeholders and beneficiaries, driving collective action and highlighting community resilience.

Partnerships among financial institutions, sovereign wealth funds like Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, and international organizations are vital. These multi-sector collaborations are key to combating desertification, restoring ecosystems, and ensuring resilient livelihoods. 🌱

Our conversations at COP16 reaffirmed this: Innovative energy finance is not just an imperative—it’s an opportunity for a resilient future. #COP16Riyadh #OurLandOurFuture #EnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment ⚡️

For the first time in 15 years, we have a new climate finance goal — but is it enough, and more importantly, does it respond to the ambitions of the UAE consensus on clean energy adopted in COP28?  🌎
 
As we close out 2024 and reflect on progress made and the work still ahead, we are sharing this special edition bulletin on financing the sustainable energy revolution 👉  https://lnkd.in/eRFEfQdq
 
The New Collective Quantified Goal adopted at COP29 committed $300 billion per year by 2035, which marks a step forward in mobilizing resources. However, developing nations need annual investment to rise from $770 billion in 2022 to $2.2–2.8 trillion by the early 2030s.
Delivering the COP28 commitments on tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency depends on bold reforms and collaborative innovation to close the energy finance gap and achieve a just energy transition. 💡
 
Beyond mobilizing private capital and creating a strong enabling environment through policy de-risking to scaling the quantity, focus must shift to the quality and impact of financing. Resources need to be accessible, strategically allocated, and equitably distributed to the regions and populations that need them most. Innovations in digital technologies, data, and AI also play a key role, reducing costs, optimizing resources, and de-risking investments. 📈
 
Happy holidays to our entire sustainable energy family! ⚡️
 
Here’s to continuing our efforts together for a just and impactful energy transition in the year to come.

2024 reminded us of the dual crises shaping our world—a record-breaking year for global temperatures and a pivotal year for renewable energy progress. Clean energy investments surpassed $2 trillion, and renewables outpaced fossil fuels. Yet, these advancements remain unevenly distributed, with low- and middle-income countries capturing only 15% of global clean energy investments (excluding China). 

This stark inequity underscores an urgent opportunity: accelerating the energy transition to drive inclusive growth and decisive climate action. 

I had the privilege of participating in the 15th IRENA Assembly on Innovative Renewables Risk Mitigation Instruments, where key stakeholders convened to explore solutions for scaling investments in underserved markets.  

💡 Key Takeaways from the Assembly: 
 
1️⃣ Lowering Financing Costs: High interest rates disproportionately impact renewable projects. Complementing fiscal strategies with non-fiscal tools—such as guarantees and concessional funding—can attract investment in high-risk markets 
2️⃣ Smarter Risk Mitigation mechanism: Governments in developing countries need support through innovative tools like green bonds, debt-for-clean-energy swaps, and public-private partnerships, which de-risk investments and attract private capital. 
3️⃣ Harnessing Digital Innovations: The integration of geospatial analytics and AI, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index, ensures smarter, data-driven investment decisions that prioritize equity and efficiency. 

As we approach major milestones like COP30 in Brazil and the G20 under South Africa’s leadership, the urgency to mobilize capital, strengthen local systems, and foster strategic partnerships cannot be overstated. 

Together, let us drive a sustainable energy revolution that bridges gaps, unlocks opportunities, and accelerates the transition to clean energy for all.

1- Lower the cost of capital for clean energy in EMDEs through de-risking mechanisms, blended finance, and performance-based instruments. 

2- Streamline international support by creating strategic alliances and deepening collaboration for bankable projects, unlocking a $65 billion investment opportunity to connect 265 million people to clean energy. 

3- Leverage tryptic of digital data and AI to optimize investment decisions, accelerating renewable projects and ensuring equitable energy access for local communities. 

Together, through smarter and more impactful investments, we can bridge the financing gap and drive an inclusive, sustainable energy transformation.

Achieving Africa’s energy and climate goals by 2030 requires over USD 200 billion in annual investments. To achieve this, we must implement clear strategies and secure increased international financial and technical support. 

I had the pleasure of meeting with Power Africa’s Cullen Hughes, Deputy Coordinator, and Carolyn Laurenzano, Development Partnerships Officer, to discuss how we can accelerate a just and equitable energy transition across the continent. Here are the key actions for progress:

1. Developing Pipeline of Bankable Projects: Initiatives like Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, and the Africa Minigrids Program, a $65 billion opportunity, are critical for bridging financing gaps. 

2. Integrated Approach to Energy Transition: Unreliable power impacts life-saving services—half of Sub-Saharan Africa’s health facilities lack reliable electricity. Through Power Africa’s the Health Electrification and Telecommunications Alliance (HETA) and UNDP's Solar for Health, we are integrating energy and health to advance universal health coverage. 

3. Innovative Financing for Off-Grid Solutions: Over 60 million people in Africa already access electricity through off-grid solutions. To accelerate energy access, we need innovative financial models and business mechanisms to scale renewable off-grid energy. 

This is a call for urgent, collective action. Together, we can drive unprecedented progress in Africa through sustainable energy transformation.

The inaugural ministerial meeting of energy ministers of the countries involved in the Southern Hydrogen Corridor #SoutH2Corridor project took place on January 21, 2025, in #Rome. 
This high-level meeting resulted in the signing of the #JointDeclaration of Political Intent for the Southern Hydrogen Corridor #SoutH2Corridor project. 

The signatory parties expressed their commitment to enhance collaboration to develop this strategic project aiming to connect production sites in Algeria to the #EuropeanUnion, by strengthening cooperation within a joint five-party working group. 

Under the Joint Declaration, the parties acknowledge the following:

-         The potential of Algeria and Tunisia in the production of renewable energy and green hydrogen, and the need to enhance energy security between the region and the European Union to foster green growth. 
-         The need for developing hydrogen stations and associated infrastructure and accelerating the sustainable energy transition to achieve global climate goals, with a focus on attracting investments in Algeria and Tunisia to bolster the local market, create jobs and promote innovation,
-         The role of the Southern Hydrogen Corridor as a key infrastructure for transporting hydrogen from Algeria through Tunisia to Europe,
-          The necessity to strengthen capacities, develop the essential skills and identify financing needs along with mechanisms for risk mitigation.

The parties pledge to collaborate on policy coordination and knowledge exchanging to ensure the effective implementation of the project, with regular assessments conducted by a joint working group that convenes every six months.

In his address, the Algerian Minister emphasized:
-         Algeria's dedication to developing the green hydrogen industry, capitalizing on its favorable geographical position, abundant solar and wind energy resources, and its well-established energy infrastructure.
-         Algeria’s ambition to establish itself as a regional hub for green hydrogen production and export to Europe, aiming to diversifying energy supplies and reducing carbon emissions.
-         The project as a strategic opportunity to enhance energy integration between Algeria and Europe, focusing on creating an effective legal and regulatory framework, developing human and technological capabilities, and attracting the necessary investments to accelerate the energy transition,
-         The importance of strengthening international cooperation to facilitate technology transfer and partnerships between the public and private sectors, 

A business forum was organized alongside the ministerial meeting, bringing together the CEOs of the involved countries’ companies to develop a roadmap outlining the future steps necessary for realizing this project. The concerned companies are #Sonatrach, #Sonelgaz, #Vng of #Germany, #SNAM of #Italy, #SEACORRIDOR (a partnership between #Eni and SNAM) and #Verbund Green Hydrogen of #Austria.

The exchange of ideas was reaffirming the vital role we all play in shaping a sustainable future.

It’s not just about entrepreneurs—it’s about all of us stepping up to drive change and reshape the energy landscape.

I also had the privilege of participating in high-level panels during the Assembly, with several key takeaways:

1️⃣ Pre-Assembly Day: The SDG7 side event emphasized the need to shift investments to the Global South, eliminate market inefficiencies, and address regulatory barriers. Supporting initiatives like Mission 300, Energy for Growth, and the Africa Minigrids Program will be critical in expanding energy access, accelerating the energy transition, and creating opportunities for inclusive growth.
2️⃣ Day 1: The Ministerial Roundtable on Scaling Up Finance for Energy Transition in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies highlighted the urgent need to bridge the financing gap for the energy transition, stressing the importance of innovative financing tools, like blended finance and de-risking mechanisms, alongside deeper collaboration to unlock opportunities.

It was also a true pleasure to reconnect with the youth leaders like Asma Rouabhia, Lydia Sanz Lozano, Josh Oxby, Sajith Wijesuriya, Kauano Moreira Chales and José Pastor. This journey has reinforced that, as young professionals, we have both the opportunity—and the responsibility—to disrupt, innovate, and lead the sustainable energy revolution.

Achieving Africa’s energy and climate goals by 2030 requires over USD 200 billion in annual investments. To achieve this, we must implement clear strategies and secure increased international financial and technical support. 

I had the pleasure of meeting with Power Africa’s Cullen Hughes, Deputy Coordinator, and Carolyn Laurenzano, Development Partnerships Officer, to discuss how we can accelerate a just and equitable energy transition across the continent. Here are the key actions for progress:

1. Developing Pipeline of Bankable Projects: Initiatives like Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, and the Africa Minigrids Program, a $65 billion opportunity, are critical for bridging financing gaps. 

2. Integrated Approach to Energy Transition: Unreliable power impacts life-saving services—half of Sub-Saharan Africa’s health facilities lack reliable electricity. Through Power Africa’s the Health Electrification and Telecommunications Alliance (HETA) and UNDP's Solar for Health, we are integrating energy and health to advance universal health coverage. 

3. Innovative Financing for Off-Grid Solutions: Over 60 million people in Africa already access electricity through off-grid solutions. To accelerate energy access, we need innovative financial models and business mechanisms to scale renewable off-grid energy. 

This is a call for urgent, collective action. Together, we can drive unprecedented progress in Africa through sustainable energy transformation. #EnergyforDevelopment #SustainableEnergyRevolution

En Colombia, 1.5 millones de personas aún viven sin acceso a electricidad, muchas en comunidades indígenas y rurales. BATx , una startup liderada por jóvenes, está cambiando esta realidad al reutilizar baterías de vehículos eléctricos para almacenamiento de energía solar.

En Katanzama, un pueblo Arhuaco en la Sierra Nevada, han instalado 40 kWh de energía limpia, llevando electricidad a una escuela, un puesto de salud y un centro cultural. 💡🏫🏥

Con el apoyo de #Youth4Climate ( UNDP Rome Centre ), Fundación Socya y otras alianzas estratégicas, este proyecto, además de llevar energía a la comunidad, también mejora el acceso a educación y salud, fortalece la resiliencia local y reduce el impacto ambiental, evitando 7 toneladas de CO₂ y 308 kg de residuos peligrosos.

World Energy Day: Ensuring Access to Sustainable Energy for All 🔋💡

With today, as World Energy Day, marked as a time to reflect on “energy efficiency and production alternatives”, it is also important to consider how we, as a global community, recognize the value and importance of sustainable energy.

The COP28 UAE Consensus to Triple Renewable capacity and Double Efficiency by 2030 sets out a clear agenda. Yet at the core of these developments are communities and people — those who still lack their fundamental right to sustainable energy.⚡️

Today, nearly:

➡️ 1.18 billion people live in energy poverty.

➡️ 685 million people live without electricity access.

➡️ 2.1 billion people lacking access to fundamental clean cooking facilities.

➡️ 2 billion people live in conflict-affected areas where energy security is critical.

➡️ Nearly 1 billion people in the Global South lack electricity in healthcare facilities.

As countries update their NDCs for COP30, and the G20 presidency seeks to mobilize finance for a just energy transition, 2025 presents a critical opportunity to move from intent to impactful action.
 
We need to ensure that resources are accessible, strategically allocated, and equitably distributed to those who need them most. Sustainable energy is not only a component of the SDG7 Agenda —“Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all” — it is also a key enabler of the entire 2030 Agenda. 🌐

Día Mundial de la Energía: Litio en América Latina y el Caribe – ¿Catalizador de una Transición Justa? 🌎 ☀️ 💡 

La transición energética es una oportunidad histórica para redefinir el rol de nuestros recursos naturales. Con más del 60% de las reservas globales de litio, la región se encuentra en una coyuntura crucial: ¿seremos simples exportadores de materia prima o líderes en la construcción de una cadena de valor regenerativa y socialmente responsable?

Como bien señala Riad Meddeb , Director del UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub , "las baterías de estado sólido podrían ofrecer un futuro más sostenible y socialmente responsable". Esta innovación abre una ventana de oportunidad para transformar la minería tradicional en una industria que impulse tanto el desarrollo tecnológico como la equidad social.

La región enfrenta un doble imperativo:
🔹Aprovechar la creciente demanda: Se proyecta que la demanda de minerales críticos se triplicará para 2030, lo que nos exige repensar nuestros modelos extractivos.
🔹Convertir ventajas geológicas en liderazgo industrial: Desde la minería responsable hasta la manufactura de tecnologías limpias, es fundamental sumar valor localmente y mitigar impactos socioambientales.

Tres pilares para una estrategia regional transformadora:
1️⃣Tecnología con propósito: Invertir en el procesamiento de litio de alta pureza, esencial para el desarrollo de baterías de estado sólido, y priorizar la eficiencia hídrica en los salares altoandinos.
2️⃣Integración regional: Coordinar políticas entre los países del "triángulo del litio" para escalar cadenas de valor y atraer inversiones responsables que impulsen la industria.
3️⃣Diálogo social vinculante: Involucrar a comunidades locales y pueblos indígenas en modelos de gobernanza que equilibren el desarrollo económico con la protección de ecosistemas.

En este Día Mundial de la Energía, recordemos que el litio no es un fin en sí mismo, sino un medio para construir sistemas energéticos más inclusivos y sostenibles. ¿Estamos preparad_s para invertir en tecnologías de procesamiento avanzado y transformar nuestro potencial en un pacto regional de progreso y justicia?

Solid-State Batteries and The Future of Mobility 🔋🚀

As we move towards a more sustainable energy future, Solid-State Batteries (SSBs) are set to transform electric vehicles; renewable energy storage; and public transport. Unlike traditional lithium-ion batteries, SSBs use a solid electrolyte as opposed to a liquid one, offering higher energy density, improved safety, and longer lifecycle.🔋

But why Solid-State Batteries?

➡️ Higher Energy Density: Delivering 5X more energy for the same weight as conventional batteries, making them ideal for industrial applications.

➡️ Faster Charging Times: Fully charged in 10-15 minutes, unlike lithium-ion batteries.

➡️ Safer and More Stable: Addressing fire and safety concerns by using non-flammable solid materials.

➡️ 30-40% Weight Reduction: Improving the overall efficiency of the devices or vehicles they power.

➡️ 10-100 Hours of Energy Storage: Important for improving grid security and building resilient infrastructures for developing countries.

➡️ Lower Carbon Footprint: Using far fewer critical minerals like cobalt & nickel, reducing their overall climate impact by up to 39%.

Find out why, with the right investments and continued innovation, a future powered by clean and renewable energy is within reach in my latest interview with Arval Mobility Observatory: 👉 https://rb.gy/7vrjft

Bridging the financing gap for sustainable development requires more than public finance alone. To unlock true economic growth, we must expand market access and mobilize private capital—especially in the world’s most underserved economies.

That’s why the United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) exists. As a hybrid development and finance institution, we deploy innovative financial tools—like guarantees, concessional loans, and investment grants—to de-risk investments and catalyze both public and private capital.

Our focus? Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States, and underserved markets—where financing gaps are widest but opportunities for impact are greatest. Through blended finance, we catalyze private investment into early-stage markets, turning them into investable opportunities.

In Tanzania, East Africa’s first subnational Green Bond—pioneered by the Government of Tanzania and now cross-listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange —demonstrates how last-mile markets, with support from de-risking institutions like the UN Capital Development Fund, can mobilize private capital. With a $1 million investment from UNCDF, the bond raised $22 million—65% from domestic investors—to finance clean water infrastructure.

Join us at the Finance in Common #FICS2025 Summit in Cape Town as we partner with Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) , Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) , Agence Française de Développement , and others to reimagine the international financial system: https://lnkd.in/e2RwkvMe

Last Friday, the Columbia Energy Association hosted the 20th annual Columbia Energy Symposium, and I did something I never thought possible. 1️⃣The Energy Transition is reshaping global supply chains and decentralizing investments, introducing new risks that financial institutions must adapt to
2️⃣ Financial institutions and governments in emerging markets need innovative tools to address the high cost of capital and limited fiscal space in these economies
3️⃣ With 1.8 billion people still lacking access to energy, the transition must go hand in hand with economic development and job creation. Philanthropy and international institutions play a critical role in unlocking energy access at scale

Not long ago, the energy sector was almost entirely male-dominated. Today, things are changing. 

Women now make up 32% of the renewable energy workforce, a significant step forward compared to traditional energy, where we are still at 22%. 

The sustainable energy revolution is not only transforming the way the world is powered—it is also creating new opportunities for us. By 2030, 18 million new clean energy jobs will be created. The question is not whether women have a place in this sector—we are already here. From leading solar initiatives in rural communities to driving innovation, advancing science, and shaping energy diplomacy, we are building the future.

But progress does not mean the work is done. Women-led startups still receive less than 3% of energy investment capital, and in many regions, women spend up to 50 hours a week gathering firewood instead of pursuing education or employment.

The transition is already happening, but it must be fair and inclusive. Creating an equitable environment at all decision-making levels is not just about fairness—it is an opportunity to unlock potential and ensure that the future truly belongs to everyone, through a just energy transition.

We have come a long way—now let’s go further. Not just today, but every day. #IWD #WomenInEnergy #SustainableFuture #JustTransition UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub Riad Meddeb Ana Victoria Rojas

⚡️From Local Action to Global Investment: Highlights from the Second Half of the 20th Annual Columbia Energy Symposium⚡️

Last Friday afternoon at the 20th Annual Columbia Energy Symposium was an energizing exploration into the financial and policy dimensions of our energy future.

The session opened with an impactful keynote by Shawyn Howard, 30th Mayor of the City of Mount Vernon, who underscored the critical role local governments play in climate action. She stressed that a data-driven narrative is essential for securing funding and urged us to engage directly with communities, through schools, local organizations, and religious spaces, to foster sustainable solutions.

In Panel Discussion 3, "Financing the Energy Transition in Emerging and Developing Markets," moderated by Muriel Jacques, Diego Mesa, Riad Meddeb, Luisa Palacios, and Suman Sureshbabu examined the challenges of high capital costs and policy barriers in developing markets. Their discussion charted a course toward unlocking the immense renewable potential in emerging markets through innovative financing approaches, risk-sharing mechanisms, and scalable investment models.

Panel Discussion 4, "Unlocking Energy Transition Through Private Capital," moderated by Heather Hartel, brought together Neil Suslak, Mekala Krishnan, Christopher Poirier, and Daniel Egan to explore how private capital can drive innovation and development of clean energy systems—reinforcing the notion that energy underpins every economic process.

The afternoon wrapped up with a stand-up live show by Rollie Williams and Matt Nelsen of Climate Town, who mixed humor with insight to tackle misinformation on wind farms and fossil fuels, ending the day on a thoughtful and uplifting note.

A heartfelt thank you to all our speakers, panelists, moderators, and the engaged audience for making the symposium's second half as inspiring and impactful as it was dynamic!

How do we solve the energy access paradox? ⚡  
 
This week, leaders at the 2025 Sustainable Energy for All Global Forum tackle this pressing question.  
 
Over 658 million people still lack electricity — 571 million in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. The regional divide is growing. Yet sustainable energy is more than a commodity; it’s key to realizing development and human rights by powering education, health, livelihoods, food and water security and more.  
 
The opportunities are clear. Universal energy access in Sub-Saharan Africa could create 4 million jobs by 2030, while technological advances make sustainable electricity the most cost-effective solution. In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, sustainable energy offers a pathway to energy independence. 
 
We know the solutions. Closing the gap by 2030 requires $30 billion annually, with half of the investments needed in Sub-Saharan Africa. Driving large-scale electrification requires unlocking technological solutions and focusing on de-risking policy and finance to attract private capital. 
 
The world cannot afford to leave 658 million people in the dark.
