1. 'Development strategies for the green hydrogen economy in emerging economies' by Fabianna Bacil, Anthony Black, Marina Domingues, Jun Jin, Rasmus Lema, Glen Robbins, Sören Scholvin. Available here: https://lnkd.in/ezcHwRpS

2. The United Nations report 'Navigating currents of Green Hydrogen Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework', by UNDP & TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, authored by Riad Meddeb, Pavel Bilek and I.
https://lnkd.in/e63jWxgb

3. 'Dismantling green colonialism: energy and climate justice in the Arab region', a book edited by hamza hamouchene and Katie Sandwell, which focuses on the politics of green extractivism with detailed cases across the Arab world. https://lnkd.in/eJK3cC2U

All three pieces are quite complementary. The first focuses on the sectoral choices and strategies pursued by different countries (Brazil, Chile, China, and South Africa) and explains differences in policies and outcomes. The second one links green hydrogen with human development needs, across energy access, environmental degradation and industrialisation, highlighting how developing nations can avoid the first mover disadvantage at the height the learning curve for H2.  The third one bring the political economy angle, the unevenness and dependencies that can created under current conditions and behaviours in green energy sectors, and provides cases that require careful examination with global relevance.

Green hydrogen can be a force for good or a terrible thing for humanity, developing nations and the planet. Whether it is one or the other will depend on how we collectively shape this agenda over the next decade.

Its promise is immense - to decarbonize heavy industry, enable green industrialization, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security - yet its trajectory remains uncertain. How can green hydrogen truly become a development pathway?
 
The task for countries is to navigate this uncertainty wisely: aligning investments with national priorities that integrate hydrogen into energy and industrial strategies which build domestic value chains, expand energy access, develop skills and jobs, and protect land, water, and biodiversity - rather than locking into extractive models.
 
Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not just markets. People must be at the center, with local value chains that create jobs and new industries. A priority of needs of the Planet must guide the use and preservation of water and land for long-term resilience. And Prosperity should be shared - with green hydrogen fueling industrialization, enhancing energy security, and decarbonizing growth.
 
Our new policy paper by UNDP and  TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, introduces this 3P approach - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to help countries steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction 👉 bit.ly/Green-H2

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Artificial intelligence is advancing at an extraordinary pace — opening a frontier that demands both imagination and responsibility. On one hand, AI holds immense potential to reshape our world. On the other, Earth’s life-support systems — climate, biodiversity, and water — are under unprecedented strain, and meeting these challenges will require ever more energy.

Global energy demand grew by 2.2% in 2024 — nearly double the recent decade’s average — with electricity consumption jumping by 4.3% as electrification, heat waves, data centers, and digitalization surged. Over the 2025–2027 period, electricity demand is expected to keep rising at around 3.9% annually.

In 2024, AI consumed 415 TWh of electricity — more than 150 individual countries. By 2030, global data center demand could reach 945 TWh, exceeding Japan’s total electricity use. Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live without reliable access to energy.

This poses an important question: what kind of intelligence are we building? Can AI learn from nature to design future energy systems that deliver a just transition?

In a reflection co-authored with Riad Meddeb , we explore the idea of Planetary Intelligence — the integration of human, technological, and natural systems to sustain habitable conditions.

Synchronize energy with the planet’s balance - AI can move beyond optimizing data centers to orchestrate energy flows as nature does — cutting grid losses, balancing renewables in real time, reducing emissions by up to 10% by 2030, and unlocking 175 GW of additional transmission capacity.

Integrating planetary health into our energy systems for smarter societies - When designed to mirror natural systems, AI can help manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity — generating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while preserving the ecosystems that sustain life.

Advancing an inclusive and equitable energy future -  From tracking bird migrations around wind farms to developing over 40 African language models, AI can amplify diverse voices and ensure that the energy transition becomes not only smarter — but also fairer and more resilient.

If AI is trained on the principles that govern life on Earth, it can help us see both the forest and the trees — guiding us toward an energy future that is more intelligent, more just, and more human.

Read more about planetary intelligence in our recent publication on Illuminem: https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

From New York Climate Week to Building Bridges, Geneva — and onwards to COP30, Belém

At the 2025 #UNGA and #ClimateWeek in New York, I was struck by the growing momentum around real solutions—those that can transform lives and protect our planet.
Among the most overdue breakthroughs: clean cooking is finally on the global agenda.

At the #SDG7ActionForum, Sheila Oparaocha of #Energia and Heather Adair-Rohani from #WHO reminded us that “clean cooking” barely captures the grim reality of dirty cooking:
- 3.2 million premature deaths every year, mostly women, more than malaria, TB, and HIV combined.
- Girls and women are risking violence while spending hours collecting firewood.
- Families trapped by the cost of charcoal, LPG, or kerosene.
- Devastating health impacts, deforestation, and biodiversity loss.

As Riad Meddeb of #UNDP noted, the case for clean cooking is undeniable:
- Dirty cooking drains US$1.4 trillion annually in health and productivity losses.
- Only 1% of clean-energy investment targets clean cooking.
- 2.5% of global greenhouse emissions come from dirty cooking, the same as the aviation sector.

There’s no reason for this to continue. The technology exists—the missing ingredients are political will and financing at scale.

At #bloomberg hosted event Mary Schapiro, Catherine McKenna, María Mendiluce reminded us of the power of women in leading for climate change. Women-led innovation should answer the call of 400 million women to access clean cooking solutions. 

As Åsa Skogström Feldt of IKEA and Yasmina Zaidman of Acumen said at #ActionSpeaks, community engagement and trust are the catalysts that make social change unstoppable, but it takes time.

Enter CleanStove.org. We are proving that the future of clean cooking is community-led, off-grid, solar-powered, and battery-driven induction: ruggedized, reliable, smoke-free, and sustainable.

Each CleanStove® enables unlimited cooking in daylight, plus up to four hours after dark, with built-in LED lighting, USB charging, and eSIM-enabled smart monitoring. The feedback from women using pilot stoves in India, Senegal and Tanzania says it all: “It's a miracle”. 

At #BuildingBridges in #Geneva, another critical link emerged: clean cooking and high-integrity carbon credits. At CleanStove®, we’re enabling verified data from every stove—uploaded and secured in Switzerland—to generate real, traceable carbon credits, converted into direct cash transfers to women who cook.

Impact finance and philanthropy both play crucial roles. CleanStove® is building partnerships to make flexible payment models—such as pay-as-you-go, leases, or loans—accessible to base-of-pyramid households.

As we head toward COP30 in Belém, Brazil, let’s make clean cooking for all not just a climate goal — but a human right.

These efforts are already accelerating - from solarizing hospitals and clinics in Yemen, to restoring decentralized power in Ukraine, to bringing renewable energy to crisis-affected communities across Sudan, Somalia, and the Sahel. Our Global #MultidimensionalPoverty Index 2025 with the Oxford Poverty & Human Development Initiative (OPHI), University of Oxford is out NOW. 

This new research finds that of 6.3 billion people in 109 countries, 1.1 billion are multidimensionally poor.

Poverty is still our greatest global challenge, which is also a challenge compounded by the climate crisis.

Of the 1.1 billion multidimensionally poor people, 887 million live in regions which are exposed to at least one of four climate hazards: high heat, drought, floods, and air pollution. 

Many poor people face overlapping climate hazards. 651 million live in regions exposed to two or more of these climate hazards, and 309 million in regions exposed to three or four climate hazards.

As climate hazards continue to grow in frequency and intensity, countries which currently have higher multidimensional poverty levels will likely experience greater average temperature increases. It is vital to align poverty reduction efforts with climate action. In the face of the climate crisis, our commitment is clear: no one must be left behind.

Read the full report below and learn more via our Human Development Report Office - United Nations Development Programme: https://go.undp.org/ioE

*A Conservation Success Story: The Resilience of Sea Turtles*

Sea turtles have long fascinated humans with their ancient lineage and majestic presence in our oceans. However, their numbers have been declining due to various threats, including overconsumption, bycatches, pollution, and habitat destruction. Nevertheless, the story of sea turtles on Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles offers a beacon of hope, demonstrating that with protection and conservation efforts, it is possible to reverse declining trends and rebuild populations. Let's explore this remarkable conservation success and the lessons it holds for protecting our planet's precious wildlife.

*A Story of Resilience and Conservation*

On Aldabra Atoll, protective measures introduced in 1968 have yielded impressive results, with over 15,000 egg clutches recorded annually between 2014 and 2019. This represents a staggering 500% increase since the 1960s, with an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 green sea turtles visiting the beaches each year to lay eggs. 

The Aldabra experience showcases the effectiveness of local conservation efforts, which can make a real difference in protecting species, while also highlighting the need for national agreements and international regulations to address broader threats.

🔵 In many crisis settings, it refers to continuity under disruption - distributed solar and storage systems keeping essential services operational amid physical and cyber risks.

🟠 In Central Asia, it implies interdependence - regional power pools projected to reduce generation costs by 8 percent through shared reserves and cross-border balancing.

🟢 In Sub-Saharan Africa, it denotes reliability - systems that can sustain demand growth and climate stress while extending access to those still excluded.

🔴 In Latin America and the Caribbean, it means protection - coastal grids redesigned with underground cabling and wind assets certified for category-five storms.

Yet, less than 1 percent of global adaptation finance is directed toward energy systems, despite investments in resilience returning multiples in gains in avoided losses and productivity.

Energy resilience binds infrastructure to governance, data to finance, and technology to social stability. In development terms, it is the capacity of an energy system to maintain function, equity, and trust when the environment around it changes.

Across Africa, the energy revolution is accelerating. Investments in renewables have nearly tripled since 2019, and solar is now the least-cost source of power in most African markets.

This transformation holds immense opportunity. Africa possesses around 60% of the world’s best solar resources, yet only 1% of installed solar capacity. Unlocking this potential could power homes and industries, create over 3 million new green jobs by 2030, and drive inclusive growth from the ground up. But for this revolution to deliver lasting development impact, it must be just - anchored in governance, innovation, and digital empowerment.

1️⃣ Strengthen Governance
Establish transparent, accountable institutions with continent-wide standards for procurement, land use, and revenue sharing to ensure renewable wealth translates into jobs, community benefits, and public trust.

2️⃣ Mobilize Innovative Finance
Move from isolated projects to bankable investment pipelines. Blended finance, risk guarantees, and local-currency mechanism can de-risk markets and crowd in private capital. By mobilizing the estimated $190 billion per year needed by 2030, African countries can power inclusive industrialization and deliver universal energy access.

3️⃣ Harness Digital, Data & AI
Leverage AI and digital tools to make systems smarter and more affordable. Predictive analytics can cut project costs by 15%, and generative AI - if locally embedded in value chains - could unlock over $100 billion in annual economic value.

Africa’s energy revolution is not a story of scarcity but one of sovereign opportunity. With the right governance, finance, and digital backbone, the continent can transform its renewable wealth into sustainable development and true energy independence.

#EnergyRevolution #JustEnergyTransition

Powershoring Finance in the Northeast of Brazil (2/3)

Building on the first round of the roundtable, this second discussion on Powershoring Finance in the Northeast of Brazil focused on the crucial role of national and subnational development banks (NDBs) in implementing financial mechanisms on the ground — opening new markets, taking on risks that commercial banks often avoid, and driving sustainable development where it matters most.

It was an honor to represent UNDP, through the Sustainable Energy Hub and the LAC EE Team, and to exchange ideas with Bruno Gabai (BNB) and Marcelo Saintive (BANDES), two key leaders in regional development finance.

💡 Key takeaways:
- Development banks have development in their DNA — they are uniquely positioned to combine financial innovation with territorial impact, supporting the green reindustrialization of the Northeast.
- We explored how to blend market-based instruments and business models with development outcomes such as job creation, social inclusion, technological advancement, and climate action.
- Subnational sovereign funds can play a pivotal role in decarbonization initiatives, for instance through the structuring of Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDCs) — a strong example of the financial innovation mindset of NDBs.
- Development impact tools are essential to design financial instruments that maximize socio-economic and environmental benefits, supporting sustainable infrastructure and powershoring.
- Constitutional and development funds, such as FNE and FDNE, remain vital sources of financing for the region’s transformation.
- National and subnational development banks can amplify their impact by channeling sovereign and non-sovereign operations from International IFIs through their structures, combining these resources with sustainable PPPs, concessions, and thematic bonds to finance powershoring and resilient infrastructure in the region.

This roundtable brought together an exceptional group of partners from international and national institutions — including UNDP, IFC, CAF, BNB, BANDES, SUDENE, FUNBIO, UnB, and ICS — under the umbrella of the event “How to Scale Up and Accelerate Sustainable Investments in the Northeast of Brazil: The Powershoring Opportunity.”

A big thank you to Banco do Nordeste (BNB), Consórcio Nordeste (CNE), and ICS for the kind invitation and continued collaboration.

The energy transition is about more than climate - it is about sustainable jobs, sovereignty, and inclusive economic growth. We need to refocus on human development at the center of energy.

Clean #energy now employs 35 million people worldwide, yet women represent only 32% of that workforce. Global investment has surpassed USD 2 trillion, outpacing fossil fuels—but translating this momentum into affordable, reliable, and inclusive energy remains the real challenge.

Smarter, decentralized systems can shift this balance. #Digital tools, #AI, and data-driven management can optimize demand, reduce losses, and improve reliability—helping every unit of energy power growth and resilience. Smarter grids alone could cut 1 gigaton of CO₂ annually and lower peak loads by 8–12% by 2050, while digitally enabled efficiency in public buildings can reduce energy use by up to 50%.

Yet energy and digital transitions are advancing faster than the systems that govern them and mitigate their risks. The priority now is pairing governance with institutional capacity and national innovation systems to make energy systems fairer, smarter, and more resilient.

This week in Skopje, I am pushing to advance these priorities during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, focusing on scaling up action toward aligning innovation, governance, and human development for a just energy future.

#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalTransition #UAEConsensus #IFESD

Globally, renewable-power capacity is projected to increase by around 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030. The opportunity now is to ensure our digital, data, and human systems can absorb this growth—by strengthening coordination, governance, and skills to drive the structural change required for a just energy transition.

Today during Day 2 of the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I moderated a discussion centered on how digitalization, data, and AI can help overcome these limits—and the new vulnerabilities they create.

1️⃣ First, the main bottleneck for renewable adoption is now absorption capacity. Grids cannot integrate trillions of USD of investment in renewables without parallel investment in #digital coordination, data systems, and human expertise. If a solar panel lacks a sensor, it effectively doesn’t exist to the system.

2️⃣ Second, #AI must remain a decision-support system, not an autonomous agent. Human oversight and digital skills are essential—especially as clean-energy jobs now account for more than half of the world’s 67 million energy-sector jobs.

3️⃣ Third, a just energy transition requires algorithmic justice. Without inclusive data governance and intentional design, algorithms trained on developed grids will reinforce the very access gaps they could help close.

4️⃣ Fourth, flexibility remains the cheapest untapped resource. Yet, fragmented regulation still blocks dynamic tariffs and peer-to-peer trading. Digital tools can help realign incentives for consumers to use energy when renewables are abundant. Unreliable grids could otherwise cost developing economies $1.3 trillion in lost output by 2030.

Ultimately, the digital, #data, and AI revolution must serve human development. These tools are already creating new market dynamics that are redefining how energy systems are governed and financed, but we need to always be vigilant to preserve our focus on what actually matters: people.

#DigitalTransition #EnergyTransition #AIForEnergy #IFESD

Today during the third day of the International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I joined young leaders for the “Youth in Energy” session to discuss their key role in shaping the revolution of energy, development, and digitalization — not as the generation of the future, but of the present. Some key actions that arose from the discussion included:

1️⃣ Invest in youth as the #digital natives of the energy transition
The world’s 1.8 billion young people are increasingly central as a creative power accelerating the energy revolution. In the Global South, entrepreneurs are three times more likely to start a business than peers in the Global North — yet over 90% of these ventures remain in informal markets. In Latin America, 36% of new entrepreneurs are under 34, but only 5% of youth-founded firms last beyond three years. Investing in reliable energy access, digital infrastructure, and early-stage finance can turn survival enterprises into scalable green innovators.

2️⃣ Build national innovation ecosystems that link ideas to markets
Youth have the creativity; what’s missing are the structures that connect their ideas to opportunity. Less than 1% of finance reaches youth-led solutions, and less than 1 in 8 young workers has formal training in green or digital skills. Governments must align education, finance, and entrepreneurship policies into national innovation ecosystems — frameworks of actors, institutions, and policies that generate, implement, and diffuse new technologies and knowledge.

3️⃣ Catalyze #youth entrepreneurship to become engines of jobs and inclusion
The task is not only to train youth but to enable them to create markets — through public procurement, incubators, and demand-driven programs. In Ghana, an agritech initiative is training 300,000 young people in AI, biotechnology, and green innovation to power modern value chains. Replicating such models can turn youth enterprises into digitally-enabled impact that can create inclusive jobs.

When young innovators can access finance and markets within larger innovation systems, they become true partners in accelerating the just energy transition.

#YouthInEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD

The energy transition is about acceleration, how quickly we can scale renewable integration. Digital, #data, and AI enable that speed — but we must not trade quickness for justice.

In Skopje this week during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, I questioned, how can we shift the conversation from digital optimization to digital integrity?

#AI can now forecast grid conditions in near real time, anticipate renewable variability, and optimize power flows across billions of data points. Predictive analytics alone could unlock 175 GW of transmission capacity and cut peak loads by 12% — proof that digital systems can make grids both efficient and smarter.

But the faster we move, the less time we leave to verify the quality, origin, and bias of the data itself. In 2024, 4,875 cyber incidents were recorded across the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors — a sharp reminder that every new sensor and data link can also be an entry point for risk. And as 83 percent of urban residents are online compared with just 48 percent of rural populations, the same connectivity gaps that divide access also shape the data that train AI models.

Without open, interoperable, and verifiable systems, we risk building a transition that is more efficient — but not more equitable.

The technologies exist. What’s missing is sustained political will and coordination to ensure that data, AI, and markets work for people, not just performance. The #energy transition will not be powered by technology alone — but by the integrity of the systems and data it rests on.

#DigitalTransition #AIforEnergy #EnergyGovernance IFESD – 14 / 14th International Forum on Energy for sustainable development _14

⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewable investment reached USD 624 billion, yet less than 15 percent reached developing economies outside China — and only 2–3 percent to Africa. 

The task ahead is not just to mobilize more capital, but to unlocking opportunities for clean energy where the need and potential are greatest. That requires financial and institutional systems capable of structuring, verifying, and absorbing investments at scale.

At the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, leaders from across regions agreed: capital follows credibility. A few ways they converged on we can do this:

1️⃣ Build national financing ecosystems, not fragmented projects, that can enable bankability of projects.
Energy-efficiency funds in Kosovo, Jordan, and Moldova show these financial mechanisms. The key for bankability starts with structuring projects with clear revenue models, transparent governance, and measurable performance to minimize investor risk.

2️⃣ Aggregate small projects to match investor logic.
Commercial lenders seek diversification. Aggregating small clean-energy projects — solar rooftops, retrofits, micro-grids — into verified portfolios lowers risk premiums and opens new credit lines for municipalities and SMEs. Inclusion also remains the ultimate de-risking strategy, as funds led by women in risk-management roles have proven on average lower default rates.

3️⃣ Embed data integrity into all financial instruments as the foundation of credibility.
Accurate baselines, open performance data, and auditability are now prerequisites for green finance. In Africa, the @AFREC Energy Information System is helping lenders quantify risk and track national progress with greater confidence. Digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can accelerate access to finance — but ensuring the datasets they are built on are equitable remains central.

The real measure of progress will be how fast we can turn global liquidity into local legitimacy — through institutions capable of absorbing, managing, and sustaining capital.

#EnergyFinance #JustEnergyTransition #FinanceForDevelopment #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD_14

Over the past days, Hurricane Melissa — one of the strongest Atlantic hurricanes on record, with wind speeds exceeding 300 km/h — has left behind devastating impacts across Caribbean’s islands, showing how climate vulnerability continues to define the frontline realities of many island nations.

Yet, amid destruction, there is also determination. Island states have long been global leaders in shaping the climate agenda — from calling for loss and damage as early as 1991, to now leading efforts toward 100% renewable energy by 2030. These ambitions are not just about technology or finance, but about shaping a different development model — one that is more inclusive, productive, and resilient.

I was pleased to represent UNDP virtually in the closing ceremony of the 10th GTI International Conference in Gozo, organized by Greening the Islands Foundation , to reflect with Edita Dranseikaite , Josianne Cutajar , Henk Rogers , camille dressler and moderated by Gianni Chianetta , on how island states can lead technologies built to resist climate vulnerabilities and inspire global solutions through a just energy transition: 

1. Integrating resilience and energy transitions.
 SIDS import around 90% of their energy as fossil fuels, often spending up to 10% of GDP annually. Transitioning to renewables could save up to USD 3.3 billion per year — roughly 3.3% of regional GDP — creating fiscal space to modernize ports, optimize grids, and strengthen essential services.

2. Financing resilience as an opportunity, not a cost.
 Every dollar invested in climate-resilient infrastructure generates about four dollars in avoided losses and economic benefits. Tailored financing mechanisms — from blended finance to de-risking instruments — can help island states attract investment while protecting communities from the next storm.

3. Harnessing digital and data intelligence.
 Digitalization is reshaping the way we plan, invest, and respond. Smart grids and AI can reduce energy losses (now equivalent to 1 gigaton of CO₂ annually) and unlock new efficiency gains.

A just energy transition is about ensuring that energy powers development across systems — water, food, health, and ecosystems. This is how island states can turn vulnerability into vision — not only bringing development to islands but bringing development from the islands. UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub Riad Meddeb

Last week, I had the opportunity to sit down with RASHID ABDALLAH, Executive Director of the African Energy Commission of the African Union  (AFREC), to discuss how data is reshaping Africa’s energy transition.

Data availability goes beyond merely monitoring progress; it plays a crucial role in de-risking investments and assisting governments and development partners in targeting projects and programs where they are most needed.

However, over 40 percent of African countries still depend on outdated or incomplete electricity data, which limits their ability to design effective policies or attract financing.

Since 2012, the African #Energy Information System, led by AFREC, has been enhancing the collection, validation, and dissemination of national energy data across the continent. Through capacity-building for national focal points, harmonization of data standards, and partnerships with regional and international organizations, AFREC is steadily improving the quality, credibility, and comparability of Africa’s energy data landscape.

In my discussion with Rashid, we explored how this initiative can align with UNDP ’s efforts to utilize geospatial analytics to move beyond binary indicators of energy access, aiming to understand how, where, and how effectively energy is used. After all, what does “access” mean if the energy is neither affordable nor reliable?

What innovations do you see as most promising for improving energy data availability? How can we ensure that #data-driven energy strategies translate into affordability, reliability, and equity?

🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt

It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries.

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt

It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries.

Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entire shipping sector today.

But hydrogen must complement—never replace—development objectives.
 
At today’s #COP30 dialogue organized by the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition  and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , I steered the discussion to explore how to ensure green hydrogen supports national development priorities, protects ecosystems, and creates shared prosperity.

1️⃣ Align hydrogen with national development priorities:
When tied to national strategies, these investments can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors and build local industry and energy security. Without this, they risk becoming extractive, with value exported and impacts retained.

2️⃣ Strengthen governance across the land–water–energy system
Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. In Namibia, a 2-million-tonne project would require 18 million m³ of water annually, equivalent to the needs of more than 250,000 people. Countries need integrated planning, clear regulation, and national innovation systems.

3️⃣ Ensure hydrogen creates local prosperity, not only export pathways:
Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.  Where hydrogen is viable, it must deliver domestic value: but in local jobs, resilient value chains, and equitable benefits.

These priorities underpin the UNDP –TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  report “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen”, which introduces a People–Planet–Prosperity framework to help countries determine where hydrogen adds genuine value: 🔗📘 bit.ly/Green-H2

Global investments in the energy transition reached a new record of USD 2.4 trillion in 2024, a 20% increase compared to the previous year. But it’s not enough to achieve the global goal of tripling renewable capacity by 2030 and it remains highly concentrated in the most advanced economies. 

The facts:

➤ Renewable energy investment reached a new record too with USD 807 billion in 2024. But year-on-year annual growth slowed, with 7.3% in 2024 compared to 32% the year before.

➤ Investment in renewable power, grids and battery storage exceeded fossil fuels investment in 2024, but fossil spending is on the rise. 

➤ Investment in energy transition technologies grew globally, but 90% remained concentrated in advanced economies and China, leaving emerging and developing countries behind. 

As leaders meet at COP30 to advance the ‘Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3 trillion’, scaling finance for emerging and developing countries is essential to make the transition truly inclusive and global.

IRENA has long called for smarter use of public funds to unlock private investment through risk-mitigation tools. The Global Landscape of Energy Transition Finance 2025 (https://lnkd.in/dmx9uuUn), a new report by IRENA and the Climate Policy Initiative shows that advanced and major economies can draw on domestic financial resources to fund energy transitions.
 
In contrast, lower-income countries depend on external support due to underdeveloped financial markets, limited fiscal capacity, high capital costs, and debt vulnerabilities amongst others. 

Find out more 👉 https://lnkd.in/dr6zZvvc

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

This affordability gap is one of the defining challenges for Africa’s economic future—but also a real opportunity to shape a new energy paradigm: one where investments are targeted, financing costs fall, and partnerships drive scalable, country-led solutions.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat, I reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to universal electrification in line with the UN-Energy Pledge. I had the pleasure to reflect with Aboubacar Said Anli, Minister of Energy, Water, and Hydrocarbons, #Comoros, Nialé Kaba, Minister of Minister of Planning and Development, #Côte d’Ivoire, Michael Franz , Team Leader, GET. Invest and moderated by Daniel Schroth Director at African Development Bank Group  , on how to ensure electricity is not only available but affordable, inclusive, and transformative:

1️⃣ Shift from counting connections to measuring development outcomes — in health, education, livelihoods, and productivity.
2️⃣ Reduce the cost of capital, which is 3–4 times higher in Africa; narrowing this gap can cut project costs by 15–25%.
3️⃣ Strengthen partnerships across governments, DFIs, development partners, and the private sector to align financing and delivery at scale.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries. #EnergyGovernance #AIandDigitalInnovation #JustEnergyTransition #UNDP COP30 Brazil

Great week in Port Moresby, where I had the privilege of co-organising with the UNDP Papua New Guinea Country Office colleagues and National Energy Authority - NEA an international conference on Advancing Energy Access: PNG Mini-grid Policy and Implementation. 

The event marked the official validation of Papua New Guinea’s Off-grid Regulation for Small Power Systems.

This regulation is a strategic lever to accelerate energy access in one of the most geographically complex contexts in the world. It provides a national framework for licensing, compliance, quality standards, and consumer protection, all essential to scaling renewable and hybrid mini-grids.

Throughout the event, we brought together institutions from the national and provincial levels, utilities, the private sector, development partners, and technical experts. The goal: move beyond policy intent and into implementation design.

To support this, I also delivered a dedicated technical training to National Energy Authority - NEA staff on the regulation’s structure, licensing pathways, dispute resolution mechanisms, tariff implications, and operationalization scenarios, equipping the institution to lead its national rollout.

Across the sessions, several priorities emerged:
🔹 Formal adoption of the regulation before December is essential to preserve regulatory continuity and unlock investment.
 🔹 NEA–PPL–province coordination mechanisms must be institutionalised, with clear roles for inspection, compliance, and system planning.
 🔹 Provincial governments and local communities must be systematically engaged, including through awareness campaigns and co-design models.
 🔹 A transparent, rule-based tariff framework must be finalised to balance cost-reflectivity with affordability, especially for low-income households.
 🔹 Private sector interest is strong — but must be matched by stability, predictability, and bankable implementation conditions.

The conference was supported by the Japan - The Government of Japan through the #PacificGreenTransformation Project, which is also advancing decentralized solar solutions in Bougainville, including innovation hubs and a flagship 1 MW mini-grid in Buin.

Green hydrogen is often presented as a technological silver bullet — but for developing countries, its real question is deeper: will it expand human development or reproduce old inequalities?

In a new UNDP–TIDE Centre report, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen, we propose a 3P Framework — People, Planet, Prosperity — to help countries steer hydrogen strategies toward development outcomes rather than extractive models.

Here are three insights shaping the debate:

👥 People: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, strengthen electricity systems, and invest in skills so workers participate in the transition — not get displaced by it.

🌍 Planet: Land, water, biodiversity and minerals face real pressures. Safeguards must come first so hydrogen supports ecological resilience instead of undermining it.

💼 Prosperity: Countries should integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, create local value chains, and move gradually — learning from early adopters to avoid first-mover risks.

The promise is real: decarbonizing heavy industry, powering green industrialisation, and creating inclusive jobs. It depends on how we govern it.

Negotiations set the ambition, but implementation will define success. To meet UAE Consensus targets, the world needs 1,122 GW of new renewables every year from 2025 — a 16.6% annual growth rate — even as 90% of renewables were cheaper than fossil fuels in 2024. The challenge isn’t only speed, but who benefits and who carries the cost of this transition.
 
The Baku-to-Belém roadmap aims to scale climate finance to $1.3T annually by 2035, triple adaptation finance, and institutionalize a Just Transition Work Program. Yet efficiency gains remain slow with only 1% improvement in 2024.
 
This is where #digitalization and #AI can accelerate progress — if designed for people and planet. The new Technology Implementation Program, especially if linked to the idea of planetary intelligence, can offer a path to align clean energy, digital systems, and nature rather than trade between them.

Green hydrogen is often presented as a technological silver bullet — but for developing countries, its real question is deeper: will it expand human development or reproduce old inequalities?

In a new UNDP–TIDE Centre report, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen, we propose a 3P Framework — People, Planet, Prosperity — to help countries steer hydrogen strategies toward development outcomes rather than extractive models.

Here are three insights shaping the debate:

👥 People: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, strengthen electricity systems, and invest in skills so workers participate in the transition — not get displaced by it.

🌍 Planet: Land, water, biodiversity and minerals face real pressures. Safeguards must come first so hydrogen supports ecological resilience instead of undermining it.

💼 Prosperity: Countries should integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, create local value chains, and move gradually — learning from early adopters to avoid first-mover risks.

The promise is real: decarbonizing heavy industry, powering green industrialisation, and creating inclusive jobs. It depends on how we govern it.

A just energy transition is not simply a technological shift. It is a development strategy. — it is social policy, industrial policy, climate policy, and a development priority all at once. 

This week, I’m with @UNDP colleagues in Dakar, Senegal, alongside 20+ country offices, energy experts, financiers and development practitioners to focus on what matters most: turning clean energy into development outcomes. 

Africa holds the world’s greatest renewable potential — including 60% of global high-quality solar and nearly 8,000 GW of solar capacity — and 30% of critical mineral reserves, positioning the continent to lead the green industrial economy.

How can we re-think Africa’s economic transformation through a just energy transition? 

Three opportunities will define its transition:
 
1️⃣ First, Africa is becoming central to the global clean-energy economy, building on green industry. Africa can go behind producing clean power — it can also industrialize it, from agro-processing to e-mobility to mineral value chains. A transformation that could save 3.7 million lives every year. 

2️⃣  Second, de-risking is essential to unlock finance at scale. Africa needs USD 190–200 billion annually for energy investment, yet risk is perceived at 2–3× reality. Blended finance, guarantees, and policy reform can flip this equation and turn pipelines into projects. 

3️⃣  Third, digitalization and AI make this transformation even more powerful, as scaling energy access is an economic imperative, which can reduce technical and commercial losses by up to 20-30%. Access must move from pilots to performance — especially for clean cooking and for deploying digital innovations that boost efficiency and productive use. 

#Digital and #AI tools can lower costs, improve planning, and support de-risking — but they are enablers, not substitutes. Community engagement, local capacity, and strong institutions remain the backbone of a just energy transition, especially where digital ecosystems are still emerging. 

Energy is ultimately about people, jobs, and dignity. This week in Dakar, with UNDP  colleagues and partners across Africa, we are working to turn the continent’s renewable wealth into universal access, green industries, and inclusive growth.

Energy took center stage during COP30 Brazil, but while the Belém Package moved negotiations forward, calls from 80+ countries to include phase-out language on fossil fuels didn’t make the final text. As SG Guterres warned — a 1.5°C overshoot is humanity’s red line.
 
Negotiations set the ambition, but implementation will define success. To meet UAE Consensus targets, the world needs 1,122 GW of new renewables every year from 2025 — a 16.6% annual growth rate — even as 90% of renewables were cheaper than fossil fuels in 2024. The challenge isn’t only speed, but who benefits and who carries the cost of this transition.
 
The Baku-to-Belém roadmap aims to scale climate finance to $1.3T annually by 2035, triple adaptation finance, and institutionalize a Just Transition Work Program. Yet efficiency gains remain slow with only 1% improvement in 2024.
 
This is where #digitalization and #AI can accelerate progress — if designed for people and planet. The new Technology Implementation Program, especially if linked to the idea of planetary intelligence, can offer a path to align clean energy, digital systems, and nature rather than trade between them.

City Future Readiness in Foreign Policy.

Thanks to our partner WeGO, the City Future Readiness Index (CFRI) has been featured in Foreign Policy Magazine.

After the successful launch of CFRI 2925 on 19 November 2025, Foreign Policy published a full article on the index and report, underlining in particular that :

1️⃣ London has been named the world’s most future-ready city in 2025, recognized for its unique blend of financial dynamism, cultural vitality, and global reach.

2️⃣ It is closely followed by San Francisco in second place, hailed as a global digital trailblazer, and Boston in third, renowned as a world-class research hub.

3️⃣ The top 10 is rounded out by global hubs Paris (4th) and New York (5th); smart, sustainable European cities Copenhagen (6th), Zurich (7th), and Stockholm (8th); and Asian innovation leaders Singapore (9th) and Seoul (10th).

The article also mentions that the CFRI distinguishes itself from other city assessment indices through its innovative, dual-structure approach. Developed by Descartes Institute in parnership with WeGO, it overcomes the limitations of opinion-survey-based indices by utilizing hard city-level data. This method ensures independence, rigor, and adaptability as data quality and coverage evolve. The index is designed as an actionable tool to better inform stakeholder decisions.

A particular attention is granted in the article to the “Metropolis Paradox” explored ion the full FCRI Report. While large, wealthy cities successfully leverage smart technologies to offset the diseconomies of scale - such as mobility and safety challenge - the report warns of a widening urban divide, calling for technological innovation, particularly the deployment of AI, to accelerate progress in urban design and management.

Another distinguishing factor of the CFRI is that it defines cities not just as narrow, single administrative units but incorporates an understanding of cities also as larger metropolitan regions or major urban centers of strategic importance for better comparison of diverse urban systems. 

In this era of rapid transition, the very definition of urban competitiveness is being reshaped. Consequently, city branding and global visibility have become crucial for those aspiring to an international role. The report also notes that talent strategies must evolve from simple attraction to facilitating “brain circulation,” while cities are increasingly building durable comparative advantages based on their unique history, culture, and experience.

🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries. #EnergyGovernance #AIandDigitalInnovation #JustEnergyTransition #UNDP COP30 Brazil

From Belém to Antalya: Anchoring Transformation in Our Shared History

Thirty years ago, I wrote my master's thesis on the vocabulary of power of Ibn Khaldun. I was captivated by how this 14th-century scholar theorized economic transformation and the conditions that enable societies to change.

I didn't expect those insights would resonate so deeply with the climate transformation challenge we face today.

Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) is perhaps the most studied scholar from the medieval Islamic world—and for good reason. He theorized economic development and societal change four centuries before Adam Smith. While his work has roots in the Muslim world, where it resonates profoundly, his insights have become universal. His work itself is a bridge between civilizations—born in North Africa, writing about societies from the Mediterranean to the Horn of Africa, offering frameworks that transcend any single tradition.

At the heart of his theory is 'asabiyyah (عصبية)—a concept often translated as "social solidarity" or "group cohesion," but which carries deeper meaning: the internal force that enables collective transformation.

Ibn Khaldun's insight was profound: Transformation doesn't come from external pressure or imposed mandates. It emerges from internal cohesion channeled through legitimate authority and grounded in economic realities.

This wasn't abstract philosophy. Ibn Khaldun was theorizing how actual societies move from one economic model to another—and why some succeed while others fracture.

As I watch today's climate debates, I keep returning to his framework:
The scale of transformation we need—from fossil fuel economies to clean energy systems—is precisely the kind of civilizational-economic shift Ibn Khaldun analyzed. Not just technical change, but transformation of how societies produce, consume, and organize themselves.

At COP30 in Belém, President Lula spoke of mutirão—collective effort. As we move toward COP31 in Antalya—a city that has itself been a bridge between continents and cultures for millennia—I wonder if Ibn Khaldun's framework might help us think more clearly about the political economy of climate transformation.

After 22 years working in sustainable development and multilateralism, I'm convinced: we need better theories of transformation, not just better targets.

Perhaps some of that wisdom has been waiting in our libraries—across cultures and centuries—for us to rediscover.

What intellectual traditions inform your thinking on transformation?

#Renewableenergy has just been named Breakthrough of the Year 2025 by Science Magazine , and the reasons are profound.

For the first time, renewables have overtaken coal as a source of global electricity. Solar and wind alone covered all growth in global electricity demand in the first half of the year. 

A few signals stand out:
1️⃣ Wind and solar are now the cheapest power sources in much of the world
2️⃣ China has scaled renewables at unprecedented speed, reshaping global supply chains
3️⃣ Rooftop solar is transforming energy access across Africa and South Asia
4️⃣ Energy security—not just climate ambition—is accelerating adoption

This progress matters not only for climate but for energy resilience, economic development, and human well-being. 

The World Meteorological Organization plays a critical role in the energy transition because renewable energy sources are inherently tied to nature’s rhythms. #WMO works with its 193 Member States to enhance the provision of high-quality, timely meteorological and climate services tailored to the energy sector. These services help governments, utilities, regulators and investors optimize renewable energy planning and operations, strengthen infrastructure resilience, and support evidence-based decisions that accelerate the energy transition and improve energy security. #WMO also contributes to global initiatives, technical guidance, capacity building, climate-energy research, and multi-partner reports that integrate climate insights into energy strategies, especially for solar, wind and hydropower. 

This means better forecasting of wind and solar resources, improved understanding of climate impacts on energy demand and supply, and smarter investment decisions that de-risk renewable deployment.

The energy transition is no longer just about decarbonisation.
It is about competitiveness, security, resilience, and development.
And that may be the real breakthrough of all.

The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of Big Data for energy and grid management. I've been getting more and more questions about what a 'smart' city looks like and wanted to re-share this article I co-authored with Calum Handforth  a while back. We argue that we need fewer 'smart' cities, and more 'smarter' cities. Smarter cities which:

* Put people at the heart of urban and technology planning and deployment. Not cities that try to retro-fit tech and energy projects and programmes around perceived citizen needs.
* Use a broad tech and innovation toolkit, and don’t just chase the latest innovation. For example, Big Data is important, but so too is the 'Thick Data' which helps us to learn more about energy consumers - or those that are energy-poor.
* Focus on outcomes, and not just the rollout of solutions - and, especially, we need ‘Smarter Cities’ which invest in the ‘connective tissue’ that creates meaningful urban spaces and places. We don’t want cities to just become ‘platforms’ of ‘use-cases’.

When writing this article, we were also inspired by the exciting and important opportunities for 'smart cities' in the Global North to learn from their counterparts in the Global South. 

And this is particularly relevant for energy, when so many innovations - including decentralised renewable energy, pay-as-you-go solar and other innovative business models, and frugal energy innovations - could be as relevant in New York as they are in New Delhi.

The latest Tracking SDG7 Progress Report reminds us that the global energy transition is not only a climate imperative but a development necessity.
 
Despite some progress, the world currently remains off track to meet #SDG7 . As of 2023, 666 million people still lack access to electricity, and 2.1 billion rely on polluting fuels for cooking. These numbers are not just statistics: they represent lost opportunities for health, education, productivity and dignity. They provide us with both a reality check and a roadmap forward - which is where our focus must be:
 
🔋 Decentralized renewable energy (DRE) is already delivering results:
Between 2020 and 2022, DRE solutions accounted for +50% of new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa. These technologies are affordable, resilient and ready to scale. With the right policy frameworks and investment flows, they can close the access gap in rural and underserved communities fast.
 
💰 Clean energy finance is growing - but it must be better targeted:
Global public finance for clean energy reached $21.6 billion in 2023, even amid economic and geopolitical instability. While incredibly promising, <10% reached EMDEs (excluding China). We need more concessional capital, blended finance models and de-risking tools to drive equitable investment where it’s needed most.
 
🍳 Clean cooking is rising on the agenda - and rightly so:
With only 7% of rural populations in Sub-Saharan Africa accessing clean fuels, now is the time to prioritize solutions that reduce health risks, empower women and support climate goals. Targeted investments in innovation and affordability can shift millions toward safer cooking practices.
 
At @UNDP, we see energy as a catalyst. Our integrated approach to sustainable energy is about more than about powering homes; it’s about unlocking futures. It’s about delivering health systems, schools, jobs, clean air, gender equality and climate resilience.
 
When we invest in energy for development, we multiply impact across the SDGs. What’s missing isn’t technology or resources: it’s urgency  and the willingness to act.  If we rise to the challenge and prioritize a just and inclusive energy transition, we can shape a future for people and planet where no one is left behind.

Over the last two days, I have been inspired by the conversations and pioneering work emerging from the IRENA Youth Forum 2026, which brings together 140 youth selected from over 26,000 applicants worldwide, convened by the International Renewable Energy Agency.

This year’s theme, “Youth Innovation and Digital Solutions: From AI to Access in Renewable Energy”, is especially fitting as the Forum is being hosted at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. Holding these discussions in a space dedicated to cutting-edge AI research reinforces a central message of the Forum: that artificial intelligence is no longer peripheral to the energy transition, but increasingly central to how energy systems are planned, governed, and deployed, particularly in developing and vulnerable contexts.

‘AI for Sustainable Energy for Development’

One of the most compelling sessions was delivered by Riad Meddeb, who explored how artificial intelligence can be leveraged to accelerate energy access and system efficiency in development contexts. What resonated most was the emphasis on governance before scale: AI’s potential to optimize grids, forecast demand, and support planning is significant, but without transparent decision-making frameworks and inclusive data ecosystems, these tools risk deepening existing inequalities. The session underscored that innovation in energy must be accompanied by accountability, institutional capacity, and human-centred design.

‘Youth Local Voices: From Local to Global Advocacy’

Equally impactful was the session led by Aitana Ramírez de Arellano Santiago, which examined how youth can translate local energy and climate challenges into credible international advocacy. The discussion moved beyond storytelling into strategy, focusing on framing, evidence, and alignment with global policy processes. For many of us working in vulnerable or under-represented contexts, the key takeaway was that local lived experience is not a limitation; when strategically framed, it is a powerful entry point into global decision-making spaces.

‘Gender and Social Impact of Renewable Energy and the Energy Transition’

The workshop facilitated by MARIA FLOUDA and Racha Moukayed McClelland offered a critical reminder that the energy transition is not only technical, but profoundly social. Discussions on gender, equity, and social outcomes highlighted that renewable energy projects can either reinforce existing power structures or actively transform them, depending on who is included in planning, ownership, and benefit-sharing. Integrating gender and social impact analysis is therefore not an add-on, but a prerequisite for a just transition.

For Small Island Developing States 🏝️, the energy transition is not just about reforming energy systems. It is about economic stability, climate resilience, and national sovereignty. With renewables now cheaper than fossil fuels across most island grids, clean energy is no longer a cost—it is the smartest macro-economic choice.

Many #SIDS import the vast majority of their energy through fossil fuels. Around 60% import at least 90% of their energy, and in countries like the Maldives, fuel imports absorb more than 10% of GDP, reaching up to 16% across SIDS in some years. This dependence exposes economies to price volatility, supply disruptions, and extreme weather.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly, I discussed how SIDS are not waiting to transition — they are already leading it. Out of necessity and innovation, they are building power systems designed for climate resilience, energy independence, and the water-energy-food nexus, from solar-powered desalination to resilient island microgrids.

The real bottleneck today is not technology — it is finance. What SIDS need are bankable investment pathways that combine concessional capital, guarantees, and risk-sharing instruments to crowd in private investors at scale. This is where digital# data and #AI become transformative: by improving demand forecasting, data transparency, grid management, and real-time performance tracking, they reduce uncertainty, lower the cost of capital, and turn small, fragmented projects into investable portfolios.

So the question is no longer whether SIDS should transition.
It is how fast we can align #finance, guarantees, and digital intelligence to unlock clean-energy investments that match their ambition — and their urgency.

The #AI era and the energy transition are advancing rapidly –– but unequally. 565 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack electricity, and 900 million rely on biomass. Whilst annual data center spending to fuel the AI boom could require investments up to USD 7 trillion by 2030.

But improving the alignment of these 21st century trends could lead to important impact. 

When planned together, digital infrastructure and AI-enabled innovation can anchor new renewable generation, create reliable offtake, and catalyze local innovation ecosystems. 

What does AI mean for development if it does not change how people access energy, cook, or economic opportunities? During a Ministerial Address at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I delved into what development-centered and meaningful AI-energy alignment looks like: 

1️⃣ AI is accelerating renewable deployment by turning planning into precision delivery: AI-enabled forecasting, digital twins, and grid analytics improve dispatch accuracy by 20-30% and cut curtailment by 10-12%, enabling faster integration of wind and solar at scale.

2️⃣ Digital systems are converting efficiency gains into fiscal space for access and inclusion: Energy inefficiency still drives nearly 60% of global energy losses, costing developing economies up to USD 1.3 trillion by 2030. Even a 10% efficiency gain, enabled by AI-based demand management and predictive maintenance, can unlock billions in savings.

3️⃣ Livelihood creation through productive use of energy: When energy and digital transitions converge, they create jobs, incomes, and development. And as clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for economic transformation.

With this emerging technology, we have the opportunity to revolutionize our energy systems, but only if AI is deliberately aligned with access, affordability, and resilience, rather than layered onto existing inequalities. The energy transition will not be driven by ambition alone—it will be shaped by whether we can turn global capital into real, investable clean-energy markets where energy demand, development needs, and climate goals intersect. 

In 2024, global investment in energy transition technologies reached a record $2.4 trillion, up 20% from 2023. Yet more than 90% of these flows went to China and advanced economies, even as fossil fuel subsidies remain at $1.1 trillion and external debt servicing reached $1.4 trillion, with 61 countries spending over 10% of public revenues just to cover interest payments.

At the UNDP  session today at the @IRENA Pavilion during #WFES2026, we focused on how to do exactly that, looking at the 3 financial solutions that unlock opportunity:

1️⃣ Strengthening local ownership and value chains is essential to turn renewable deployment into development. In regions such as North Africa, capacity is scaling rapidly, but external ownership and export-oriented models limit job creation, skills, and domestic value capture.

2️⃣ Using debt-smart and blended finance instruments can restore fiscal space for clean energy. In non-oil-producing MENA countries, debt-to-GDP ratios approaching 90% are crowding out public investment in energy, health, and education—making guarantees, concessional capital, and debt-linked climate finance critical.

3️⃣ De-risking and demand-anchoring mechanisms can lower the cost of capital. Today, renewable projects in high-risk markets face financing costs two to three times higher than in advanced economies, even though the technologies are the same.

These realities point to a simple truth: scaling clean energy without reforming financial systems will reproduce inequality. The future of a just transition lies in what we learn - and change - when capital is structured to reduce risk, retain value locally, and support inclusive investment, energy solutions become affordable, resilient, and scalable—making a just energy transition the engine for development pathways that are truly sustainable.

Clean cooking needs $8 billion a year to reach universal access – but we’re mobilizing barely a third of that. This isn’t just a funding gap. It’s a development failure.  

As I said early today: “We’re paying trillions of dollars to avoid spending billions." 

At what point do we stop calling this an “investment gap” when the cost of doing nothing is a thousand times higher? 

The numbers speak for themselves: 

➡️ $2.4 trillion – the estimated annual cost of dirty cooking in terms of healthcare, environmental degradation, and lost productivity. 

➡️ $2.5 billion - the total annual investment currently going into clean cooking solutions. That’s not even a third of what’s needed to achieve universal access by 2030. 

This is not an “investment gap.” It’s a missed opportunity to align climate, health, gender equity, and economic development goals through a single intervention. To change the trajectory, we need to shift the financing paradigm. Here are three catalytic approaches leading the way: 

1️⃣ Blended finance: Combining grants, guarantees, and concessional capital to de-risk private investment, reduce end-user costs, and help early-stage enterprises scale. 

2️⃣ Digital pay-as-you-go systems: Leveraging mobile payments and smart tech to improve affordability, enable real-time monitoring, and unlock access to carbon and impact finance. 

3️⃣ Outcome-based financing: Linking investor returns directly to measurable social and health results, shifting focus from inputs to verified impact. 

At UNDP, we’re advancing these models through Financial Innovation Labs, turning clean cooking from a development afterthought into core climate and infrastructure investment opportunities. Let’s de-risk, digitize, and diversify. Clean cooking is not a side issue; it's a frontline solution for sustainable development. #EnergyforDevelopment #CleanCooking

I really enjoyed recording this pod with my friend and colleague, Siddharth Singh . In it, we went through the three distinct phases of global energy demand over the last 50 years:

1) 1970s - 2000s: OECD dominance. In the mid-70s the OECD accounted for around 80% of global GDP. This was reflected in energy consumption skewed towards these richer countries, where the energy intensive materials needed for cities and industries were concentrated.

2) Early 2000s to the present day: The rise of China. In just three decades, China's urban population has grown by 600 million people. It has added 300 million cars to the road, built 37,000 km of highspeed rail (4x the entire European total), and used more cement in two years than the US did over the entirety of the 20th century. This needed A LOT of energy, propelling China right to the top of the energy consumption league. In the last decade alone, China accounted for more than half of global oil and gas demand growth and 60 of electricity demand growth. 

3) The future: China's working age population, its cement production and its steel output have all peaked. In the next 20 years, India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America could add 3x times the number of people to their urban populations as China did over the last decade. Rising wealth, access rates, and demand for services like cooling and water desalination that are exacerbated by rising temperatures and climate change, will all lead to a further shift in the geography of global energy demand. 

Happy listening!

We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equivalent to a trillion gigabytes, we often hear data being called the the new oil, gold, or currency. But data only creates value when it is translated into decisions. 

Data centres already consume 1.5–2% of global electricity, rising to 5–20% in major digital hubs, while putting growing pressure on power systems, water, and land. 

At the same time, when the just energy transition and the digital revolution are planned together, clean power and data reinforce each other. When clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for jobs, livelihoods, and sustainable development — not just electrons.

This is why, at UNDP , we are working closely with governments and energy partners to turn data into a development asset for the AI and energy transition. Earlier today, at #WFES2026 we reflected on what we are learning in practice. 
Three strategic insights stand out:

1️⃣Data, digital and AI are now a core asset for clean energy investment and delivery. High-quality energy data can de-risk projects and attract capital — but only if digital energy systems are cyber-secure. As grids become digital, cybersecurity becomes energy security, protecting hospitals, water systems, and local businesses. Geospatial and context-specific data can significantly improve energy planning, identify viable investments, and accelerate rollout.

2️⃣ Focus must shift from data systems to data ecosystems. Energy solutions increasingly generate data, but transformational impact depends on how these data flow across institutions, sectors and stakeholders. Building inclusive energy ecosystems requires systems-level approaches; linking data, energy priorities and development objectives, from national policy to local delivery.	

3️⃣ Data transparency and accountability can make energy systems inclusive. Our data shows 447 million “electrified” people do not actually use power. When energy data is transparent and well-governed, utilities and investors become accountable for who is served and who is left behind — turning energy systems into platforms for livelihoods and inclusive development, not just grid connections.

As we move deeper into the AI and energy transition, the real challenge is not generating more data - but using it effectively and governing it better, together. The future of the energy transition will be shaped not by how much data we generate, but on whether data systems reflect lived realities, enable better decisions, and align digital innovation with equitable energy outcomes
